cases.summary: Picasso painted a huge anti-war canvas after the bombing of the Basque town of Guernica.
cases.takeaway: Art can respond to current events.

cases.summary: Marcel Duchamp submitted a signed urinal to an exhibition, asking what counts as art.
cases.takeaway: Context and idea can define a work.

cases.summary: Girl with Balloon self-shredded moments after selling at Sotheby's for about £1 million, and was renamed Love is in the Bin.

cases.summary: UK voters chose to leave the EU by 51.9% to 48.1%, beginning a long withdrawal process.
cases.takeaway: Referendums can reshape alliances.
cases.title: Brexit referendum

rows: China, France, Russia, United Kingdom, United States
tables.title: UN Security Council

cases.summary: After the bloody Kalinga war, Emperor Ashoka embraced Buddhism and promoted non-violence and tolerance.
cases.takeaway: Religion can shape statecraft.
cases.title: Ashoka's conversion

cases.summary: Martin Luther's Ninety-five Theses, spread by the printing press, split Western Christianity.
cases.takeaway: Technology amplifies religious change.
cases.title: The Protestant Reformation

cases.summary: A Chicago gathering brought Eastern and Western religious leaders together, including Swami Vivekananda.
cases.takeaway: Interfaith dialogue has a long history.
cases.title: Parliament of the World's Religions

tables.title: Share of world population, 2020 (Pew Research Center estimates)

cases.summary: An Italian worker, Vincenzo Peruggia, took the painting from the Louvre in Paris; it was found two years later, and the news made it the most famous painting in the world.
cases.takeaway: Fame can come from an unexpected event.
cases.title: The Mona Lisa is stolen

cases.summary: Four teenagers and a dog found a cave in France full of paintings of horses, deer and bulls made about 17,000 years ago.
cases.takeaway: People have made art for tens of thousands of years.
cases.title: The caves of Lascaux

rows: Orange (red + yellow), green (yellow + blue), purple (blue + red)
tables.title: Colour mixing

cases.summary: Antonie van Leeuwenhoek, a Dutch cloth merchant, made powerful single-lens microscopes and was the first to see bacteria, which he called 'animalcules'.
cases.takeaway: A better tool can reveal a whole new world.
cases.title: Leeuwenhoek's tiny animals

cases.summary: James Watson and Francis Crick built a model of DNA as a double helix, using X-ray pictures taken by Rosalind Franklin and Maurice Wilkins.
cases.takeaway: Teamwork and data from many scientists led to the discovery.
cases.title: The shape of DNA
cases.wiki: Molecular Structure of Nucleic Acids: A Structure for Deoxyribose Nucleic Acid

tables.title: Levels of organisation in living things

cases.summary: Dmitri Mendeleev arranged the known elements by atomic mass and left gaps for elements not yet discovered; later discoveries, such as gallium and germanium, matched his predictions.
cases.takeaway: A good pattern can predict the unknown.
cases.title: Mendeleev's periodic table

cases.summary: Marie and Pierre Curie discovered the elements polonium and radium; Marie Curie won Nobel Prizes in both physics (1903) and chemistry (1911).
cases.takeaway: Careful, patient work can open a new field of science.
cases.title: Marie Curie and radioactivity

rows: Takes the shape of its container
Close together, slide past each other
tables.title: The three common states of matter

cases.summary: Ada Lovelace wrote a method for Charles Babbage's planned Analytical Engine to calculate Bernoulli numbers, often called the first computer program.
cases.takeaway: She saw that machines could work with more than numbers.
cases.title: Ada Lovelace's first program

cases.summary: Operators of the Harvard Mark II found a moth stuck in a relay and taped it into the log book as the 'first actual case of bug being found'.
cases.takeaway: Debugging means finding and fixing faults.
cases.title: The first computer bug

cases.summary: Louis Pasteur showed that heating wine and milk gently kills the microbes that spoil them, which made food safer and last longer.
cases.takeaway: Heat can make food safe.
cases.title: Pasteurisation

cases.summary: Ship's doctor James Lind gave different treatments to sailors with scurvy; those who ate oranges and lemons recovered fastest, and later sailors carried citrus to prevent the disease.
cases.takeaway: A fair test can show which food helps health.
cases.title: James Lind and scurvy

cases.summary: Statistician Abraham Wald realised that armour should go where returning bombers had no bullet holes, because planes hit there never made it home.
cases.takeaway: Think about what you are not seeing.
cases.title: The airplane armour puzzle

cases.summary: A New York newspaper printed a series of stories claiming an astronomer had seen bat-winged creatures on the Moon; many readers believed them.
cases.takeaway: Check the source before you believe a story.
cases.title: The Great Moon Hoax

rows: Attacking the person instead of the idea
'Everyone does it, so it must be right'
Pretending there are only two options
Judging all from a few examples
tables.title: Spotting weak arguments

cases.summary: Prices of tulip bulbs in the Netherlands soared to enormous levels and then collapsed in February 1637, an early example of a speculative bubble.
cases.takeaway: Prices can rise far above the real value of something.
cases.title: Tulip Mania

cases.summary: After the US stock market crash of 1929, banks failed, businesses closed and about a quarter of American workers lost their jobs.
cases.takeaway: Economies can fall quickly and take years to recover.
cases.title: The Great Depression

rows: Tools and machines used to make things
Taking a risk to start a business
tables.title: Factors of production

cases.summary: Johannes Gutenberg printed Bibles using movable metal type, making books faster and cheaper to produce; within fifty years printed books were common across Europe.
cases.takeaway: Printing spread reading and ideas.
cases.title: The Gutenberg Bible

cases.summary: Two of Shakespeare's fellow actors collected 36 of his plays into one book, saving about half of them that might otherwise have been lost.
cases.takeaway: Books keep stories alive.
cases.title: Shakespeare's First Folio

rows: Names a person, place or thing
tables.title: Parts of speech

cases.summary: Shares in the South Sea Company rose from about £128 to about £1,000 in a few months and then crashed; many investors lost their savings.
cases.takeaway: If something sounds too good to be true, be careful.
cases.title: The South Sea Bubble

cases.summary: Muhammad Yunus started lending very small amounts to poor villagers in Bangladesh, mostly women, so they could start tiny businesses; he won the Nobel Peace Prize in 2006.
cases.takeaway: Small loans can help people build a living.
cases.title: The Grameen Bank

cases.summary: Dr Henry Heimlich described abdominal thrusts as a way to clear a blocked airway; the technique is still taught to help people who are choking.
cases.takeaway: A simple skill can save a life.
cases.title: The Heimlich manoeuvre

cases.summary: Putting automated defibrillators in airports, stations and sports halls has allowed bystanders to restart hearts in the first minutes after a cardiac arrest.
cases.takeaway: Every minute counts, so quick action matters.
cases.title: Defibrillators in public places

rows: Send for help (call the emergency number)
Start CPR if not breathing normally
tables.title: DRSABCD: what to do in an emergency

cases.summary: A stone carved with the same decree in Greek and two Egyptian scripts let Jean-François Champollion work out how to read hieroglyphs in 1822.
cases.takeaway: Comparing languages can unlock lost ones.
cases.title: The Rosetta Stone

cases.summary: United States Marines used the Navajo language as a spoken code in the Pacific during the Second World War, and enemy codebreakers never cracked it.
cases.takeaway: Languages carry culture and can protect messages.
cases.title: The Navajo code talkers

cases.summary: Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin landed on the Moon in Apollo 11 while Michael Collins stayed in orbit; about 600 million people watched on television.
cases.takeaway: Big goals need teamwork.
cases.title: The first Moon landing

cases.summary: Crowds crossed from East to West Berlin after the border opened, and Germany became one country again in October 1990.
cases.takeaway: Change can come quickly.
cases.title: The fall of the Berlin Wall

rows: Largest continent by area and population
Includes Canada, the USA and Mexico
tables.title: The seven continents

cases.summary: Rivers feeding the Aral Sea in Central Asia were diverted to irrigate cotton, so the sea shrank to a small fraction of its size.
cases.takeaway: Using water in one place can harm another.
cases.title: The Aral Sea

cases.summary: The 82 km canal across Panama let ships sail between the Atlantic and Pacific without going around South America, saving about 13,000 km.
cases.takeaway: Engineering can reshape trade routes.
cases.title: The Panama Canal

cases.summary: After a worldwide vaccination campaign, the World Health Organization announced in 1980 that smallpox, which had killed millions of people, was gone.
cases.takeaway: Vaccines and teamwork can wipe out a disease.
cases.title: The end of smallpox

cases.summary: Doctor John Snow marked cholera deaths on a map of London, saw they clustered around one water pump, and persuaded officials to remove its handle.
cases.takeaway: Careful observation can protect health.
cases.title: John Snow and the water pump

cases.summary: A student at UCLA tried to send the word 'LOGIN' to a computer at Stanford; the system crashed after the letters 'LO', but the connection worked later that night.
cases.takeaway: Big networks start with small steps.
cases.title: The first message on the Internet

cases.summary: Tim Berners-Lee at CERN made the first website public, explaining the World Wide Web project.
cases.takeaway: Sharing ideas openly helped the Web grow.
cases.title: The first website
cases.wiki: History of the World Wide Web

cases.summary: The Prophet Muhammad and his followers moved from Mecca to Medina; the Islamic calendar starts from this event.
cases.takeaway: An important event can mark the start of a calendar.
cases.title: The Hijra

cases.summary: In Baghdad, scholars translated books from Greek, Persian and Indian into Arabic and added their own discoveries in mathematics, astronomy and medicine.
cases.takeaway: Sharing knowledge across cultures advances science.
cases.title: The House of Wisdom

rows: Pilgrimage to Mecca once in a lifetime, if able
tables.title: The Five Pillars of Islam

cases.summary: Euclid organised geometry into definitions, rules and step-by-step proofs; his book was used to teach geometry for more than 2,000 years.
cases.takeaway: Mathematics is built on clear reasoning.
cases.title: Euclid's Elements

cases.summary: Leonardo of Pisa, called Fibonacci, wrote Liber Abaci, which taught Europeans the Hindu–Arabic numerals (0–9) used today.
cases.takeaway: Good ideas travel along trade routes.
cases.title: Fibonacci brings numbers to Europe

cases.summary: Ludwig van Beethoven, almost completely deaf, took part in the first performance of a symphony with a choir; its 'Ode to Joy' is now the anthem of Europe.
cases.takeaway: Creativity can overcome great difficulties.
cases.title: Beethoven's Ninth Symphony

cases.summary: Stravinsky's new, rhythmic music and dance caused an uproar in the audience at its first performance in Paris, but it is now a classic.
cases.takeaway: New art can shock before it is accepted.
cases.title: The Rite of Spring

rows: Blowing across or through a reed
tables.title: Instrument families of the orchestra

cases.summary: Athens put the philosopher Socrates on trial for questioning accepted beliefs; he chose to accept the death sentence rather than leave the city.
cases.takeaway: Asking hard questions can be risky but valuable.
cases.title: The trial of Socrates

cases.summary: Philippa Foot asked whether you should divert a runaway trolley to save five people if it would harm one; it is still used to explore moral choices.
cases.takeaway: Thought experiments test our moral ideas.
cases.title: The trolley problem

cases.summary: Roger Bannister ran a mile in 3 minutes 59.4 seconds, after many people believed it could not be done; others soon followed.
cases.takeaway: Training and belief can break barriers.
cases.title: The four-minute mile

cases.summary: Jesse Owens won four gold medals at the Berlin Olympics, in front of a regime that preached racial superiority.
cases.takeaway: Sport can challenge prejudice.
cases.title: Jesse Owens in Berlin

cases.summary: Galileo pointed a telescope at the sky and saw mountains on the Moon and four moons orbiting Jupiter, evidence that not everything circles the Earth.
cases.takeaway: Observation can change how we see the universe.
cases.title: Galileo's telescope

cases.summary: Astronaut David Scott dropped a hammer and a feather together on the Moon; with no air, they hit the ground at the same time.
cases.takeaway: Without air resistance, all objects fall at the same rate.
cases.title: Hammer and feather on the Moon

cases.summary: Louis Pasteur boiled broth in flasks with long, curved necks that let air in but kept dust out; the broth stayed clear, showing that germs come from the air, not from nothing.
cases.takeaway: A clever experiment can settle a long debate.
cases.title: Pasteur's swan-neck flasks

cases.summary: Arthur Eddington photographed stars near the Sun during a total eclipse; their light was bent as Einstein's theory predicted.
cases.takeaway: Scientists test ideas with observations.
cases.title: The eclipse that proved Einstein

rows: Test it with a fair experiment
Draw a conclusion and share it
tables.title: Steps of the scientific method

cases.summary: English barons forced King John to agree that even a king must obey the law; the document inspired later ideas of rights and fair trials.
cases.takeaway: Leaders are not above the law.
cases.title: Magna Carta

cases.summary: After Rosa Parks refused to give up her bus seat in Montgomery, Alabama, African Americans boycotted the buses for 381 days until segregated seating was ended.
cases.takeaway: Peaceful action can change unfair rules.
cases.title: Rosa Parks and the bus boycott

rows: Explains the laws and settles disputes
tables.title: Three branches of government

cases.summary: When ice crushed his ship near Antarctica, Ernest Shackleton led all 28 men to safety, including a 1,300 km lifeboat journey to South Georgia.
cases.takeaway: Good leadership and teamwork help people survive.
cases.title: Shackleton's Endurance expedition

cases.summary: After an explosion on the way to the Moon, the crew and engineers on the ground improvised a way to clean the air and return home safely.
cases.takeaway: Stay calm and use what you have.
cases.title: Apollo 13

cases.summary: A plague spread along trade routes and killed an estimated third or more of Europe's people; with fewer workers, wages rose and old ways of life changed.
cases.takeaway: Disease can change societies.
cases.title: The Black Death

cases.summary: The last Western Roman emperor was removed from power in 476, while the Eastern Roman (Byzantine) Empire lasted until 1453.
cases.takeaway: Empires rise and fall.
cases.title: The fall of the Western Roman Empire
cases.wiki: Fall of the Western Roman Empire

cases.summary: George Smith read a clay tablet in the British Museum and found a flood story much older than the one in the Bible.
cases.takeaway: Old stories connect cultures.
cases.title: Reading the Epic of Gilgamesh

cases.summary: Shakespeare's friends printed 36 of his plays in one book, saving many that might have been lost.
cases.takeaway: Printing preserves stories.
cases.title: The First Folio

rows: Collected in the Middle East over many centuries
tables.title: Stories from around the world

cases.summary: Aristotle argued that the good life comes from developing virtues, such as courage, as a mean between extremes of deficiency and excess.
cases.takeaway: Character is built by habit.
cases.title: Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics

cases.summary: Jean-Paul Sartre's Paris lecture set out the claim that 'existence precedes essence': we are not born with a fixed purpose and must create our own.
cases.takeaway: Freedom brings responsibility.
cases.title: Sartre's 'Existentialism Is a Humanism'

cases.summary: Edmund Gettier's three-page paper gave cases where someone has a justified true belief that is not knowledge, challenging the standard definition of knowledge.
cases.takeaway: A short paper can overturn an old definition.
cases.title: The Gettier problem

cases.summary: A cannon fired during a performance of Henry VIII set the thatched roof of Shakespeare's Globe on fire and burned the theatre down; it was rebuilt within a year.
cases.takeaway: Theatres are shaped by the buildings they perform in.
cases.title: The Globe Theatre fire

cases.summary: Each year over a million Muslims, around 2.5 million in 2019, gather at Mecca for the pilgrimage that every able Muslim should make once in a lifetime.
cases.takeaway: One of the world's largest annual gatherings tests logistics and safety planning.
cases.title: The Hajj

cases.summary: DJ Kool Herc's party at 1520 Sedgwick Avenue in the Bronx, where he extended instrumental breaks, is widely cited as the beginning of hip-hop.
cases.takeaway: Cultural movements start in small, local scenes.
cases.title: The birth of hip-hop

cases.summary: Louis Armstrong's Hot Five and Hot Seven recordings in Chicago shaped jazz by making the improvised solo central.
cases.takeaway: Recordings spread musical innovation worldwide.
cases.title: Louis Armstrong's Hot Five

cases.summary: In On Liberty, John Stuart Mill argued that society may restrict a person's freedom only to prevent harm to others.
cases.takeaway: A limit on state power that still shapes law.
cases.title: Mill's harm principle

cases.summary: In The Republic, Plato imagines prisoners who mistake shadows on a wall for reality, and one who escapes to see the sun, an image of philosophical education.
cases.takeaway: Appearance and reality may differ.
cases.title: The Allegory of the Cave

cases.summary: Johannes Gutenberg printed about 180 copies of the Bible with movable metal type in Mainz; within fifty years millions of books had been printed in Europe.
cases.takeaway: Print cut the cost of ideas.
cases.title: The Gutenberg Bible

cases.summary: Under the third caliph Uthman, an official written copy of the Qur'an was prepared and copies were sent to major cities to standardise the text.
cases.takeaway: Written standardisation preserved a shared text.
cases.title: The standard codex

cases.summary: Scholars in Baghdad translated Greek, Persian, Sanskrit and Syriac works into Arabic, preserving and advancing science and philosophy.
cases.takeaway: Translation can carry knowledge across civilisations.
cases.title: The translation movement

tables.title: Abbasid milestones

cases.summary: Hernán Cortés and his indigenous allies captured the Aztec capital after a siege, helped by epidemic smallpox.
cases.takeaway: Disease and alliances decided the conquest.
cases.title: Fall of Tenochtitlan

cases.summary: The Qhapaq Ñan linked the Inca Empire across the Andes, spanning tens of thousands of kilometres.
cases.takeaway: Roads bind empires.
cases.title: The Inca road system

cases.summary: After 1085, scholars in Toledo translated Arabic works on astronomy, medicine and philosophy into Latin, feeding European universities.
cases.takeaway: Cultural contact moves knowledge.
cases.title: Toledo's translators

rows: Abd al-Rahman III proclaims the Caliphate of Córdoba
tables.title: Al-Andalus timeline

cases.summary: Genentech scientists made human insulin in E. coli in 1978; Humulin was approved in 1982 as the first genetically engineered human medicine.
cases.takeaway: Bacteria can be factories for human proteins.
cases.title: Human insulin from bacteria

cases.summary: Matthias Schleiden and Theodor Schwann proposed that all organisms are made of cells (1838–39), and Rudolf Virchow added that new cells come only from existing cells (1855).
cases.takeaway: The cell is the basic unit of life.
cases.title: Cell theory

cases.summary: Once numbering billions, passenger pigeons were hunted to extinction; the last one, Martha, died at the Cincinnati Zoo.
cases.takeaway: Even abundant species can vanish quickly.
cases.title: The last passenger pigeon

cases.summary: After the five-year voyage of HMS Beagle (1831–1836), Charles Darwin published his theory of natural selection; the first print run of 1,250 copies sold out on the first day.
cases.takeaway: Variation plus selection explains the diversity of life.
cases.title: On the Origin of Species

cases.summary: By growing bacteria in heavy and light nitrogen, Matthew Meselson and Franklin Stahl showed that DNA replicates semi-conservatively: each new molecule keeps one old strand.
cases.takeaway: An elegant experiment settled how DNA copies itself.
cases.title: The Meselson–Stahl experiment

cases.summary: In regions with malaria, carrying one sickle-cell allele protects against severe malaria, so the allele stays common despite harming people with two copies.
cases.takeaway: Selection can maintain harmful alleles when heterozygotes benefit.
cases.title: Sickle-cell and malaria

cases.summary: Edward Jenner inoculated eight-year-old James Phipps with cowpox material and showed he was then protected from smallpox, starting vaccination.
cases.takeaway: A deliberate, safer exposure can train immunity.
cases.title: Jenner's smallpox vaccine

cases.summary: Gregor Mendel crossed about 28,000 pea plants and found that traits are inherited in discrete units, with a 3 : 1 ratio in the second generation. His work was rediscovered in 1900.
cases.takeaway: Heredity follows statistical rules.
cases.title: Mendel's pea experiments

cases.summary: An iron rod blew through the front of railway foreman Phineas Gage's skull; he survived, and reports of his personality change helped link the frontal lobes to behaviour.
cases.takeaway: Injuries gave early evidence of brain function.
cases.title: Phineas Gage

cases.summary: Jan Baptist van Helmont grew a willow in a weighed pot of soil for five years; the tree gained about 74 kg while the soil lost only about 57 g, showing that plants build mass mainly from water (and, as later learned, from carbon dioxide).
cases.takeaway: Plants make their mass from air and water, not soil.
cases.title: Van Helmont's willow experiment

cases.summary: Carl Linnaeus's Systema Naturae organised living things in a hierarchy and, by 1753, gave each species a two-part Latin name such as Homo sapiens.
cases.takeaway: A shared naming system lets scientists communicate.
cases.title: Linnaeus's binomial names

cases.summary: Dmitri Ivanovsky and Martinus Beijerinck found an infectious agent smaller than bacteria in 1892–98; Wendell Stanley crystallised it in 1935, showing viruses are particles.
cases.takeaway: A new class of infectious agent was discovered.
cases.title: The tobacco mosaic virus

cases.summary: After the Airbus crashed in the Atlantic in June 2009, a Bayesian search plan combining prior probabilities with failed searches located the wreck in April 2011.
cases.takeaway: Bayesian search turns negative results into information.
cases.title: Finding Air France Flight 447

cases.summary: John Craven's team used Bayesian search theory to locate the lost submarine.

cases.summary: The Nasdaq Composite peaked at 5,048 on 10 March 2000 and then lost about 78% of its value by October 2002.
cases.takeaway: Overconfidence and herding inflate bubbles.
cases.title: The dot-com bubble

cases.summary: Daniel Kahneman, a psychologist, shared the economics Nobel for prospect theory.
cases.takeaway: Psychology belongs in economic models.

cases.summary: John Goodenough, Stanley Whittingham and Akira Yoshino won the Chemistry Nobel for developing lithium-ion batteries, now in phones and electric vehicles.

cases.title: The lithium-ion battery

cases.summary: Henry Le Chatelier showed that a system at equilibrium shifts to oppose a change in concentration, pressure or temperature, a principle used to maximise yields in industry.
cases.takeaway: Equilibrium can be steered.

cases.summary: Jacques Charles launched an unmanned hydrogen balloon from Paris; his work on how gas volume changes with temperature gave Charles's law.
cases.takeaway: Gas behaviour is predictable from pressure, volume and temperature.
cases.title: The first hydrogen balloon flight

cases.summary: Paul Anastas and John Warner set out twelve principles, such as preventing waste and using safer solvents, to design chemical processes that reduce harm.
cases.takeaway: Prevention is better than clean-up.
cases.title: The twelve principles of green chemistry

cases.summary: Combining nitrogen and hydrogen under high pressure with an iron catalyst makes ammonia for fertiliser; it is estimated to help feed roughly half the world's population.
cases.takeaway: One reaction transformed agriculture.

cases.summary: The Avogadro constant was fixed at exactly 6.02214076 × 10²³ per mole when the SI base units were redefined.
cases.takeaway: Counting atoms by weighing relies on a fixed number.

cases.summary: Friedrich Wöhler made urea, an organic compound found in urine, from inorganic ammonium cyanate, challenging the idea that living things had a special 'vital force'.
cases.takeaway: Organic compounds obey the same chemistry as everything else.
cases.title: Wöhler's urea synthesis

cases.summary: Dmitri Mendeleev left gaps in his periodic table and predicted the properties of undiscovered elements; gallium (1875), scandium (1879) and germanium (1886) matched closely.
cases.takeaway: A good model predicts what has not yet been found.
cases.title: Mendeleev's predictions

cases.summary: A leak of methyl isocyanate from a pesticide plant in Bhopal, India killed thousands within days; official figures count about 3,800 immediate deaths and estimates of total deaths are far higher.
cases.takeaway: Safety systems and maintenance are essential in hazardous industries.
cases.title: The Bhopal disaster

cases.summary: Germain Hess showed that the heat of a reaction is the same whether it happens in one step or several, which lets chemists calculate energies they cannot measure directly.

cases.takeaway: Targeting a cancer's molecular cause works.

cases.summary: Cells taken without consent from Henrietta Lacks became the first immortal human cell line and underpinned many discoveries.
cases.takeaway: Research ethics and consent matter.

cases.summary: Charles Keeling's measurements on Mauna Loa show atmospheric CO₂ rising from about 315 ppm in 1958 to over 420 ppm in the 2020s.
cases.takeaway: Long, careful measurement revealed human influence.
cases.title: The Keeling Curve

cases.summary: 196 parties adopted the first universal climate agreement, entering into force in November 2016.
cases.takeaway: Voluntary pledges plus transparency can unite nearly every country.
cases.title: Paris Agreement

cases.summary: AlexNet cut the top-5 error on ImageNet to 15.3%, against 26.2% for the runner-up, launching the deep-learning era.
cases.takeaway: GPUs plus big data made deep networks practical.

cases.summary: Elinor Ostrom, the first woman to win the economics Nobel, showed communities can govern shared resources without privatisation or state control.
cases.takeaway: Tragedy of the commons is not inevitable.
cases.title: Ostrom's Nobel Prize

formulas.expr: With zero transaction costs, bargaining yields an efficient outcome whatever the initial rights
formulas.label: Coase theorem

cases.summary: When the Soviet Union blockaded West Berlin, Western allies flew in food and fuel for almost a year.
cases.takeaway: Logistics can be a form of resistance.
cases.title: Berlin Airlift

cases.summary: European powers met in Berlin to set rules for claiming African territory without African representation; by 1914 nearly all of Africa was colonised.
cases.takeaway: Borders drawn abroad shaped later conflicts.
cases.title: Berlin Conference

cases.summary: DeepMind's AlphaFold 2 predicted protein structures with a median accuracy near experimental quality (GDT ≈ 92); Hassabis and Jumper shared the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry with David Baker.
cases.takeaway: Machine learning solved a 50-year grand challenge.

cases.summary: Bednorz and Müller found superconductivity in a copper oxide near 35 K, far above earlier limits, and won the 1987 Nobel Prize.
cases.takeaway: Unexpected materials open new physics.
cases.title: High-temperature superconductivity

cases.summary: He Jiankui announced the birth of gene-edited twins; he was sentenced to three years in prison in December 2019.
cases.takeaway: Germline editing raises unresolved ethical and safety issues.
cases.title: The CRISPR babies

cases.summary: Casgevy for sickle-cell disease and beta-thalassaemia was approved in the UK and then the US.
cases.takeaway: Gene editing has moved from lab to clinic.

cases.takeaway: Weak key procedures break strong machines.
cases.title: Breaking Enigma

cases.summary: Rivest, Shamir and Adleman published public-key encryption, years after the British GCHQ had secretly invented the same idea.
cases.takeaway: Public-key cryptography enabled secure e-commerce.

cases.summary: Customs investigators found about 1,400 works in the Munich flat of Cornelius Gurlitt, including art with suspected Nazi-era looting links.
cases.takeaway: Provenance research is ongoing work.

cases.summary: Alexander Fleming noticed a mould that killed bacteria; Florey and Chain developed it into a drug in the 1940s, and the three shared the 1945 Nobel Prize.
cases.takeaway: Chance observations need persistent follow-up.

cases.summary: US house prices fell, leveraged mortgage securities lost value, and Lehman Brothers failed on 15 September 2008, freezing credit worldwide.
cases.takeaway: Interconnected leverage spreads local losses into global crises.
cases.title: The 2008 financial crisis

cases.summary: After years of recession and a peso fixed to the dollar, Argentina defaulted on about $93 billion of debt, at the time the largest sovereign default in history.
cases.takeaway: Fixed exchange rates can become a trap.
cases.title: Argentina's 2001 default

cases.summary: Kenneth Arrow proved that no ranked voting system can satisfy a short list of fairness conditions with three or more options.
cases.takeaway: Every voting system makes trade-offs.
cases.title: Arrow's impossibility theorem

cases.summary: Thailand floated the baht on 2 July 1997; currencies and stock markets across East Asia collapsed, and the IMF arranged rescue packages with strict conditions.
cases.takeaway: Short-term foreign debt and pegged currencies are fragile.
cases.title: The Asian financial crisis

cases.summary: About three million people died in Bengal; Amartya Sen argued that falling entitlements to food, not just supply, caused famine.
cases.takeaway: Famines can occur even when food exists.
cases.title: The Bengal famine

cases.summary: After cutting interest rates close to zero, the US Federal Reserve bought trillions of dollars of bonds to lower long-term rates and support the economy.
cases.takeaway: Central banks developed new tools when rates hit zero.
cases.title: Quantitative easing

cases.summary: Prime Minister Robert Peel repealed tariffs on imported grain, a landmark victory for free trade in Britain.
cases.takeaway: Trade policy shifts income between landowners and consumers.
cases.title: The repeal of the Corn Laws

cases.summary: Satoshi Nakamoto mined the first Bitcoin block, with a message about bank bailouts embedded in it, beginning a decentralised digital currency.
cases.takeaway: New money forms challenge central-bank control.
cases.title: Bitcoin's launch

cases.summary: The Nasdaq peaked at 5,048 on 10 March 2000 and then lost about 78% of its value by October 2002.
cases.takeaway: Valuations must eventually be supported by earnings.
cases.title: The dot-com bubble

cases.summary: Abhijit Banerjee, Esther Duflo and Michael Kremer won the economics Nobel for using randomised experiments to test anti-poverty programmes.
cases.takeaway: Experiments show what works, not just what sounds plausible.
cases.title: Randomised trials in development

cases.summary: Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, Hong Kong and Singapore combined high savings, export promotion and education to grow around 7–10% a year for decades.
cases.takeaway: Policy and investment in people can speed development.
cases.title: The East Asian miracle

cases.summary: Short-run demand for oil was inelastic, so a supply cut raised prices roughly fourfold and total revenue for exporters rose.
cases.takeaway: Inelastic demand gives sellers pricing power.
cases.title: OPEC and inelastic demand

formulas.label: Price elasticity of demand
formulas.note: |Eₚ| > 1: elastic;  |Eₚ| < 1: inelastic

cases.summary: Acts of Parliament fenced off common land into private farms, raising farm output but pushing many rural poor into towns and wage labour.
cases.takeaway: Property rights reshape who benefits from land.
cases.title: The enclosure movement

cases.summary: The US Clean Air Act Amendments of 1990 created a sulfur-dioxide permit market that cut power-plant emissions faster and more cheaply than predicted.
cases.takeaway: Markets can be designed to price pollution.
cases.title: Cap-and-trade for acid rain

cases.summary: The 2009 US stimulus package of about $800 billion aimed to raise demand during the Great Recession; economists still debate the size of its multiplier.
cases.takeaway: The size of the multiplier depends on spare capacity.
cases.title: The fiscal multiplier

formulas.label: Simple spending multiplier
formulas.note: MPC is the marginal propensity to consume

cases.summary: Milton Friedman argued that inflation is always a monetary phenomenon; Paul Volcker's tight money policy cut US inflation from about 13% in 1980 to under 4% by 1983.
cases.takeaway: Controlling money growth can end inflation, at a cost in unemployment.
cases.title: Friedman's monetarism

cases.summary: Simon Kuznets built the first US national income accounts for Congress in 1934; GDP became the standard measure after Bretton Woods in 1944.
cases.takeaway: What we measure shapes what we try to grow.
cases.title: Measuring national income

formulas.label: GDP by expenditure
formulas.note: Consumption, investment, government spending and net exports

cases.summary: Eastern marks were exchanged for West German marks at 1:1 for wages and many savings in July 1990; East German industry struggled and large transfers followed.
cases.takeaway: A favourable exchange rate raised living standards but hurt competitiveness.
cases.title: German reunification

cases.summary: Muhammad Yunus's bank lent small sums to poor borrowers, mostly women, in groups; Yunus and the bank shared the 2006 Nobel Peace Prize.
cases.takeaway: Small loans can help, but are not a cure for poverty.
cases.title: The Grameen Bank

cases.summary: High-yield wheat and rice varieties, fertiliser and irrigation, pioneered by Norman Borlaug, raised grain yields and helped India and Mexico avoid famine.
cases.takeaway: Technology can raise food supply but with environmental costs.
cases.title: The Green Revolution

cases.summary: Friedrich Hayek argued that prices carry dispersed knowledge no central planner can collect.
cases.takeaway: Prices coordinate information across millions of people.
cases.title: Hayek and the knowledge problem

cases.summary: The US Bureau of Labor Statistics has published the Consumer Price Index since 1913; it prices a fixed basket of goods over time.
cases.takeaway: Price indexes track changes in the cost of living.
cases.title: Measuring inflation

cases.summary: George Akerlof showed that when sellers know more about quality than buyers, bad used cars can drive good ones out of the market; he shared the 2001 Nobel Prize.
cases.takeaway: Hidden information can make markets fail.
cases.title: The market for lemons

cases.summary: Written in the Great Depression, it argued that governments should spend to raise demand when private spending collapses.
cases.takeaway: Recessions need not fix themselves.
cases.title: Keynes and The General Theory
cases.wiki: The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money

cases.summary: Studies find each extra year of schooling raises earnings by roughly 8–10% on average, partly through skills and partly through signalling.
cases.takeaway: Education is both an investment and a signal.
cases.title: The returns to education

cases.summary: Mexico announced in August 1982 that it could not meet its debt payments; many Latin American countries then went through a 'lost decade' of low growth.
cases.takeaway: Borrowing in foreign currency leaves countries exposed to interest-rate shocks.
cases.title: The Latin American debt crisis

cases.summary: Thomas Malthus argued that population grows geometrically but food supply only arithmetically, leading to famine; technology later raised food output far more than he expected.
cases.takeaway: Forecasts based on fixed technology can be badly wrong.
cases.title: Malthus's population principle

cases.summary: Marx argued that profit comes from surplus value, the labour workers perform beyond what is needed to pay their wages.
cases.takeaway: A theory of capitalism that inspired political movements worldwide.
cases.title: Das Kapital

cases.summary: Comparing fast-food restaurants in New Jersey and Pennsylvania after New Jersey raised its minimum wage, David Card and Alan Krueger found no fall in employment.
cases.takeaway: Natural experiments can overturn textbook predictions.
cases.title: Card and Krueger on the minimum wage

cases.summary: When banks lend out deposits, the same money is deposited again, so a deposit can support several times its value in total deposits.
cases.takeaway: Banks create money by lending.
cases.title: The money multiplier

formulas.label: Money multiplier
formulas.note: A 10% reserve ratio gives a multiplier of 10 in the simplest model

cases.summary: The US Supreme Court ordered Standard Oil, which controlled most US refining, to be broken into 34 companies under the Sherman Act.
cases.takeaway: Antitrust law limits market power.
cases.title: Standard Oil breakup

cases.summary: A run on New York trust companies was stopped when J. P. Morgan organised private bankers to lend funds; the crisis led to the creation of the US Federal Reserve in 1913.
cases.takeaway: A lender of last resort prevents bank runs from spreading.
cases.title: The Panic of 1907

cases.summary: Thomas Piketty used tax records over centuries to argue that when returns on capital (r) exceed growth (g), wealth concentrates.
cases.takeaway: Data over long periods can change policy debates.
cases.title: Capital in the Twenty-First Century

cases.summary: Russia freed most prices in January 1992 and privatised state firms; inflation exceeded 2,000% that year and output fell sharply before recovering after 1999.
cases.takeaway: Rapid transition can bring severe short-term costs.
cases.title: Russia's shock therapy

cases.summary: Finance ministers of France, West Germany, Japan, the UK and US agreed to push down the overvalued US dollar; the dollar fell sharply against the yen and mark over the next two years.
cases.takeaway: Coordinated intervention can move exchange rates.
cases.title: The Plaza Accord

cases.summary: The Economist created the Big Mac index to compare currencies using the price of a burger as an informal test of purchasing power parity.
cases.takeaway: Price gaps hint at over- or undervalued currencies.
cases.title: The Big Mac index

formulas.label: Absolute purchasing power parity
formulas.note: Exchange rate equals the ratio of price levels

cases.summary: Garrett Hardin argued that shared resources are overused when no one owns them; Elinor Ostrom later showed that many communities manage commons successfully.
cases.takeaway: Rules and communities can protect shared resources.
cases.title: The tragedy of the commons

cases.summary: Oil became over 90% of Nigeria's export earnings, leaving the economy vulnerable to price swings and weakening other sectors ('Dutch disease').
cases.takeaway: Natural riches do not guarantee development.
cases.title: The resource curse in Nigeria

cases.summary: Ricardo showed that England and Portugal both gain by trading cloth and wine even if Portugal makes both more efficiently, because of different opportunity costs.
cases.takeaway: Countries gain by specialising in what they give up least to produce.
cases.title: Ricardo's wine and cloth

cases.summary: Joseph Schumpeter described capitalism as constantly destroying old industries as new ones arise, as when digital cameras replaced film.
cases.takeaway: Innovation brings growth and disruption together.
cases.title: Creative destruction

cases.summary: In The Wealth of Nations Smith described ten workers dividing pin-making into about 18 steps and producing around 48,000 pins a day, against perhaps one, and certainly not twenty, for a person working alone.
cases.takeaway: Specialisation raises productivity.
cases.title: Adam Smith's pin factory

cases.summary: Robert Solow found that most US output growth could not be explained by more capital and labour, pointing to technology.
cases.takeaway: Ideas, not only inputs, drive growth.
cases.title: The Solow residual

formulas.label: Solow capital accumulation
formulas.note: Capital per worker settles where saving equals depreciation plus population growth

cases.summary: Shares in the South Sea Company rose from about £128 in January to about £1,000 in June 1720 and then crashed; Isaac Newton reportedly lost a large sum.
cases.takeaway: Even brilliant people can be caught in a bubble.
cases.title: The South Sea Bubble

cases.summary: The US raised tariffs on over 20,000 goods; trading partners retaliated and world trade fell sharply over the next few years.
cases.takeaway: Tariff wars can deepen downturns.
cases.title: The Smoot–Hawley Tariff

cases.summary: Prices of tulip bulb contracts in the Dutch Republic soared and then collapsed in February 1637, often cited as an early speculative bubble, though historians debate how large the damage was.
cases.takeaway: Rising prices can feed on themselves until confidence breaks.
cases.title: Tulip Mania

cases.summary: People are counted as unemployed only if they are jobless and actively looking for work, so discouraged workers who have stopped searching do not appear in the headline rate.
cases.takeaway: Headline rates can hide hidden slack.
cases.title: Counting the unemployed

formulas.label: Unemployment rate

cases.summary: The VOC issued shares traded on the Amsterdam exchange, making it one of the first publicly traded companies.
cases.takeaway: Joint-stock companies spread risk and funded global trade.
cases.title: The Dutch East India Company

cases.summary: Germany printed money to pay reparations and debts; by November 1923 one US dollar was worth about 4.2 trillion marks, and a new Rentenmark ended the crisis.
cases.takeaway: Loss of fiscal credibility feeds on itself.
cases.title: Hyperinflation in Weimar Germany

cases.summary: Printing money to fund deficits drove inflation to an estimated 79.6 billion percent a month in November 2008; the central bank issued a 100-trillion-dollar note before the currency was abandoned in 2009.
cases.takeaway: Monetising deficits destroys a currency.
cases.title: Zimbabwe's hyperinflation

cases.summary: Wolves were reintroduced after about 70 years; scientists documented changes in elk behaviour and vegetation, though the size of the 'trophic cascade' is debated.
cases.takeaway: Top predators can reshape ecosystems.
cases.title: Wolves return to Yellowstone

cases.summary: Tuvalu's highest point is only about 4.6 m above sea level; global sea level has been rising by roughly 3–4 mm a year in recent decades, threatening low-lying nations.
cases.takeaway: Small island states are on the front line of climate change.
cases.title: Tuvalu and rising seas

cases.summary: Every few years warm water spreads across the eastern Pacific, shifting rainfall and fisheries; the 1997–98 event was among the strongest on record.
cases.takeaway: Ocean cycles drive weather across continents.
cases.title: El Niño

cases.summary: The 82-kilometre canal cut the sea journey between the Atlantic and Pacific by about 13,000 km; its construction cost the lives of an estimated 25,000 workers.
cases.takeaway: Engineering can reshape world trade routes.
cases.title: The Panama Canal opens

cases.summary: NASA launched the first Earth-resources satellite, beginning the longest continuous record of Earth's surface from space.
cases.takeaway: Satellites turned geography into a data science.
cases.title: Landsat 1

cases.summary: Alfred Wegener proposed that continents move, citing matching fossils and coastlines. Most geologists rejected him until seafloor-spreading evidence in the 1960s established plate tectonics.
cases.takeaway: A correct idea can wait decades for a mechanism.
cases.title: Wegener's continental drift

cases.summary: A container ship ran aground and blocked the Suez Canal for six days, holding up hundreds of ships and showing how much trade depends on a few chokepoints.
cases.takeaway: Supply chains depend on narrow passages.
cases.title: The Ever Given blocks the Suez Canal

cases.summary: A magnitude 9.1–9.3 earthquake off Sumatra triggered a tsunami that killed about 230,000 people in 14 countries and led to a regional warning system.
cases.takeaway: Early warning and preparedness save lives.
cases.title: The 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami

cases.summary: The Philippine eruption injected sulfur dioxide into the stratosphere and cooled the Earth's surface by about 0.5 °C for around two years.
cases.takeaway: Large eruptions can change global climate.
cases.title: The eruption of Mount Pinatubo

cases.summary: Johann von Thünen modelled farmland around a market town as concentric rings, with perishable and bulky goods grown closest to the market.
cases.takeaway: Transport costs shape land use.
cases.title: Von Thünen's rings

cases.summary: Game theorists including Paul Milgrom, Robert Wilson and Preston McAfee designed the US simultaneous multiple-round auction for radio spectrum, raising billions.
cases.takeaway: Good market design is applied game theory.
cases.title: FCC spectrum auctions
