cases.takeaway: A planet-sized network of telescopes imaged an event horizon.
cases.title: First image of a black hole

cases.summary: Two teams observing distant supernovae found the expansion of the Universe is speeding up; Perlmutter, Schmidt and Riess won the 2011 Nobel Prize.
cases.takeaway: Dark energy was discovered by observation.
cases.title: Accelerating Universe

formulas.label: Schwarzschild radius
formulas.note: Sun ≈ 2.95 km

formulas.expr: v = H₀ · d,  H₀ ≈ 70 km s⁻¹ Mpc⁻¹
formulas.label: Hubble's law
formulas.note: Measurements still disagree between about 67 and 73

cases.summary: Student protests in Paris, the Prague Spring, anti-war and civil-rights movements in the US, and the Tlatelolco massacre in Mexico City marked a year of worldwide unrest.
cases.takeaway: Youth movements challenged governments on several continents at once.
cases.title: The global protests of 1968

cases.summary: Louis XIV ruled France for 72 years and moved his court to Versailles in 1682, drawing nobles under royal control.
cases.takeaway: Display and ritual can be tools of power.
cases.title: Louis XIV and Versailles

cases.summary: Aksum minted its own coins and traded ivory and gold from its Red Sea port of Adulis; King Ezana adopted Christianity in the 4th century.
cases.takeaway: Trade connected the Horn of Africa with Rome and India.
cases.title: The Kingdom of Aksum

cases.summary: Alexander built an empire from Greece to India and died in Babylon aged 32; successor kingdoms spread Greek culture across the region.
cases.takeaway: Conquest can spread culture even when the empire breaks up.
cases.title: Alexander the Great

cases.summary: The thirteen colonies declared independence from Britain, citing Enlightenment ideas of natural rights; the Treaty of Paris recognised the United States in 1783.
cases.takeaway: Revolutionary ideas crossed the Atlantic in both directions.
cases.title: The Declaration of Independence

cases.summary: Nelson Mandela was released on 11 February 1990 after 27 years in prison; South Africa's first multiracial elections on 27 April 1994 made him president.
cases.takeaway: Negotiation and sanctions helped end legal racial segregation.
cases.title: The end of apartheid

cases.summary: A Tunisian street vendor's self-immolation in December 2010 sparked protests that toppled leaders in Tunisia, Egypt, Libya and Yemen. Outcomes ranged from reform to civil war.
cases.takeaway: Social media and economic grievance can mobilise mass protest, but not guarantee democracy.
cases.title: The Arab Spring

cases.summary: Beginning with arrests of Armenian leaders in Constantinople on 24 April 1915, the Ottoman government deported and killed an estimated one million or more Armenians.
cases.takeaway: It helped inspire the term 'genocide' and later legal definitions.
cases.title: The Armenian genocide

cases.summary: After the bloody Kalinga war, Ashoka promoted dhamma (moral conduct) through edicts carved on rocks and pillars across his empire.
cases.takeaway: Rulers can use public inscriptions to shape values.
cases.title: Ashoka's edicts

cases.summary: Cleisthenes reorganised Athens so that citizens (free adult men) took part in the Assembly and Council; women, slaves and foreigners were excluded.
cases.takeaway: Early democracy was real but narrow.
cases.title: Cleisthenes' reforms

cases.summary: Twenty-nine Asian and African nations met in Indonesia and rejected being pawns of the superpowers; the Non-Aligned Movement was founded in Belgrade in 1961.
cases.takeaway: Newly independent states sought a third path in the Cold War.
cases.title: The Bandung Conference

cases.summary: Plague spread along trade routes, reached Mediterranean ports in 1347 and killed an estimated third or more of Europe's people. Labour shortages raised wages and weakened feudal ties.
cases.takeaway: Pandemics reshape economies and social order.
cases.title: The Black Death

cases.summary: Delegates created the IMF and World Bank in July 1944 and pegged currencies to the US dollar, which was convertible to gold. President Nixon ended convertibility on 15 August 1971.
cases.takeaway: Fixed exchange-rate systems depend on confidence in the anchor.
cases.title: The Bretton Woods system

cases.summary: Emperor Justinian I commissioned the Corpus Juris Civilis, the foundation of civil-law systems, and rebuilt the Hagia Sophia, completed in 537.
cases.takeaway: Law and architecture projected imperial authority.
cases.title: Justinian's Code and Hagia Sophia

cases.summary: Deng Xiaoping's reforms, including household farming and special economic zones such as Shenzhen (1980), helped China's economy grow about 9–10% a year for three decades.
cases.takeaway: Gradual market reform can transform an economy.
cases.title: China's reform and opening

cases.summary: Potatoes, maize and tomatoes reached Europe and Asia, and horses, wheat and sugar reached the Americas, while epidemic diseases devastated Indigenous populations.
cases.takeaway: Exchange between hemispheres changed diets and populations worldwide.
cases.title: The Columbian Exchange

cases.summary: Peter Safar and others combined mouth-to-mouth ventilation with chest compressions, forming the basis of modern CPR.
cases.takeaway: Immediate bystander CPR improves survival.
cases.title: Modern CPR is born

cases.summary: After Pope Urban II's call in 1095, Western knights captured Jerusalem in July 1099 and founded Crusader states that lasted until 1291.
cases.takeaway: Religion, politics and trade all drove the Crusades.
cases.title: The First Crusade

cases.summary: A 13-day standoff over Soviet missiles in Cuba ended when the USSR agreed to remove them; the US publicly pledged not to invade Cuba and privately agreed to remove missiles from Turkey.
cases.takeaway: Back-channels and face-saving exits can prevent nuclear war.
cases.title: The Cuban Missile Crisis

cases.summary: Rebels led by Fidel Castro entered Havana on 1 January 1959, and Cuba soon allied with the Soviet Union.
cases.takeaway: A revolution on the US doorstep intensified the Cold War.
cases.title: The Cuban Revolution

cases.summary: Led by Kwame Nkrumah, the Gold Coast became the first sub-Saharan African colony to gain independence; 17 African countries became independent in 1960.
cases.takeaway: Independence movements spread quickly after 1957.
cases.title: Ghana's independence

cases.summary: Drought and the plowing of prairie grassland caused huge dust storms, such as Black Sunday on 14 April 1935; about 2.5 million people left the Plains states.
cases.takeaway: Poor land use can turn drought into disaster.
cases.title: The Dust Bowl

cases.summary: Denis Diderot and Jean d'Alembert edited 28 volumes of the Encyclopédie to gather and spread knowledge based on reason.
cases.takeaway: Ideas spread by print challenged traditional authority.
cases.title: The Encyclopédie

cases.summary: Six countries created the European Economic Community in 1957; the Maastricht Treaty founded the EU in 1992, and euro notes and coins entered circulation in 2002.
cases.takeaway: Economic integration was used to secure peace.
cases.title: From the Treaty of Rome to the euro

cases.summary: Spain and Portugal divided newly reached lands along a line west of the Cape Verde Islands, which later gave Portugal claim to Brazil.
cases.takeaway: European powers carved up the world by treaty.
cases.title: The Treaty of Tordesillas

cases.summary: Fascist blackshirts marched toward Rome and King Victor Emmanuel III invited Benito Mussolini to form a government, beginning two decades of dictatorship.
cases.takeaway: Economic crisis and weak institutions can open the door to dictators.
cases.title: Mussolini's March on Rome

cases.summary: William the Conqueror ordered a survey of landholdings in England, recording who held what land and how much it was worth.
cases.takeaway: Record-keeping underpins taxation and state power.
cases.title: The Domesday Book

cases.summary: An H1N1 influenza virus infected about a third of the world's population and killed an estimated 50 million people.
cases.takeaway: Troop movements and crowded cities helped it spread worldwide.
cases.title: The 1918 influenza pandemic

cases.summary: The Bastille was stormed on 14 July 1789 and the Declaration of the Rights of Man was adopted in August; the Reign of Terror in 1793–94 saw about 17,000 official executions.
cases.takeaway: Revolutions can radicalise and devour their own.
cases.title: The French Revolution

cases.summary: After wars against Denmark (1864), Austria (1866) and France (1870–71), Prussia under Bismarck proclaimed the German Empire at Versailles on 18 January 1871.
cases.takeaway: Nation-building by war and diplomacy.
cases.title: The unification of Germany

cases.summary: Under the Guptas, scholars such as Aryabhata advanced astronomy and mathematics, and the decimal place-value system with zero spread.
cases.takeaway: Mathematical ideas travel with trade and scholarship.
cases.title: India's classical age

cases.summary: Enslaved people in Saint-Domingue, led by figures such as Toussaint Louverture, defeated colonial armies; Haiti declared independence on 1 January 1804 as the first Black republic.
cases.takeaway: The only successful large-scale slave revolt created a nation.
cases.title: The Haitian Revolution

cases.summary: Hammurabi of Babylon had 282 laws carved on a stone stele, setting penalties that differed by social class; it is now in the Louvre.
cases.takeaway: Written, public law limits arbitrary rule.
cases.title: The Code of Hammurabi

cases.summary: A network of north German and Baltic merchant towns, led by Lübeck, protected trade in timber, grain, furs and fish.
cases.takeaway: Merchant cooperation can rival kingdoms.
cases.title: The Hanseatic League

cases.summary: One of the Indus cities had grid-planned streets, brick-lined drains and standardised bricks; its script remains undeciphered.
cases.takeaway: Early cities had sophisticated planning without surviving written histories.
cases.title: Mohenjo-daro

cases.summary: Mechanised textiles, James Watt's improved steam engine (patented 1769) and the factory system began in Britain and spread to Europe, the US and Japan, drawing people into cities.
cases.takeaway: New technology reshapes production, cities and class.
cases.title: The Industrial Revolution

cases.summary: Mass protests forced Shah Mohammad Reza Pahlavi to leave in January 1979; Ayatollah Khomeini returned and an Islamic republic was declared in April.
cases.takeaway: Broad coalitions can topple a strong state.
cases.title: The Iranian Revolution

cases.summary: After Israel's declaration of independence on 14 May 1948, neighbouring Arab states intervened; about 700,000 Palestinians fled or were expelled, an event known as the Nakba.
cases.takeaway: The war created a refugee problem that remains unresolved.
cases.title: The 1948 Arab–Israeli War

cases.summary: Banking wealth of the Medici family funded artists such as Brunelleschi, Donatello and Botticelli, helping make Florence the heart of the Renaissance.
cases.takeaway: Patronage and commerce can drive a cultural flowering.
cases.title: Florence and the Medici

cases.summary: Garibaldi's Expedition of the Thousand (1860) and Cavour's diplomacy led to the Kingdom of Italy, proclaimed on 17 March 1861; Rome joined in 1870.
cases.takeaway: Nationalism could unite scattered states.
cases.title: The unification of Italy

cases.summary: Husayn ibn Ali and his followers were killed by Umayyad forces; Shia Muslims commemorate the day as Ashura.
cases.takeaway: A succession dispute became a lasting religious division.
cases.title: The Battle of Karbala

cases.summary: North Korea invaded the South in June 1950; UN forces led by the US and, later, Chinese troops joined. An armistice in July 1953 left the peninsula divided near the 38th parallel.
cases.takeaway: A Cold War proxy conflict ended without a peace treaty.
cases.title: The Korean War

cases.summary: Bolívar led campaigns that freed Venezuela, Colombia, Ecuador, Peru and Bolivia from Spain, but his plan for a united Gran Colombia broke up in 1831.
cases.takeaway: Independence did not guarantee unity.
cases.title: Simón Bolívar

cases.summary: The Mali emperor travelled to Mecca through Cairo with a vast caravan; his lavish gold spending reportedly depressed gold prices in Cairo for years.
cases.takeaway: West African wealth was known across the Mediterranean world.
cases.title: Mansa Musa's pilgrimage

cases.summary: The US gave about $13 billion to rebuild Western Europe, helping restore trade and political stability.
cases.takeaway: Aid can rebuild markets and strengthen alliances.
cases.title: The Marshall Plan

cases.summary: Samurai reformers overthrew the Tokugawa shogunate and restored imperial rule, then built a modern army, railways and a constitution (1889).
cases.takeaway: State-led modernisation made Japan an industrial power within decades.
cases.title: The Meiji Restoration

cases.summary: Admiral Zheng He led seven treasure fleets to Southeast Asia, India, Arabia and East Africa, with ships far larger than European ones of the time; the Ming then turned inward.
cases.takeaway: A strong navy did not become a lasting maritime empire.
cases.title: Zheng He's voyages

cases.summary: Monumental carved stone circles in southeastern Turkey were built by hunter-gatherers before farming began, challenging the idea that settled life came first.
cases.takeaway: Ritual and community may have driven early settlement.
cases.title: Göbekli Tepe

cases.summary: Non-nuclear states promised not to acquire nuclear weapons and nuclear states promised to work toward disarmament. India, Pakistan and Israel never joined, and North Korea announced withdrawal in 2003.
cases.takeaway: Arms-control treaties limit but do not stop proliferation.
cases.title: The Non-Proliferation Treaty
cases.wiki: Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons

cases.summary: Arab OPEC members cut oil exports to countries supporting Israel in the Yom Kippur War; prices roughly quadrupled and Western economies suffered stagflation.
cases.takeaway: Energy dependence is an economic and political weakness.
cases.title: The 1973 oil embargo

cases.summary: Britain fought China over the opium trade; the Treaty of Nanjing ceded Hong Kong and opened treaty ports to foreign trade.
cases.takeaway: Trade disputes backed by force reshaped China's sovereignty.
cases.title: The First Opium War

cases.summary: British India was divided into India and Pakistan. An estimated 10–20 million people were displaced and hundreds of thousands to about a million died in the violence.
cases.takeaway: Hasty borders and communal tension can cause mass tragedy.
cases.title: The Partition of India

cases.summary: Sparta and its allies defeated Athens after a long war, ending Athenian dominance of Greece; Thucydides wrote its history.
cases.takeaway: Prolonged war can destroy a democratic power.
cases.title: The Peloponnesian War

cases.summary: Cyrus the Great founded the empire in 550 BCE; provinces (satrapies), the Royal Road and tolerance of local customs helped govern millions of people.
cases.takeaway: Tolerance and communication lines can hold a vast empire together.
cases.title: Persian royal administration

cases.summary: After defeating Nationalist forces in the civil war, Mao Zedong proclaimed the People's Republic in Beijing; the Nationalists retreated to Taiwan.
cases.takeaway: Land reform and military victory remade China.
cases.title: Founding of the People's Republic of China

cases.summary: Hannibal crossed the Alps and crushed Rome at Cannae in 216 BCE, but Scipio defeated him at Zama in 202 BCE, making Rome master of the western Mediterranean.
cases.takeaway: Strategy can win battles; resources win wars.
cases.title: Hannibal and the Second Punic War

cases.summary: King Zheng of Qin completed the conquest of rival states, standardised writing, weights and currency, and began linking northern walls. The Qin fell in 206 BCE and the Han followed.
cases.takeaway: Standardisation unifies, but harsh rule can be short-lived.
cases.title: Qin Shi Huang unifies China

cases.summary: A mutiny of sepoys in the East India Company's army spread into a wider revolt; afterwards the British Crown took direct rule in 1858.
cases.takeaway: Rebellion led to a change of colonial system, not an end to it.
cases.title: The Indian Rebellion of 1857

cases.summary: Within about 20 years of Muhammad's death, armies of the Rashidun caliphs controlled Arabia, Syria, Egypt, Iraq and Persia, ending the Sasanian Empire in 651.
cases.takeaway: A new religious community expanded with remarkable speed.
cases.title: The early Muslim conquests

cases.summary: According to tradition, Martin Luther posted his theses against the sale of indulgences in Wittenberg; the printing press spread his ideas across Europe within weeks.
cases.takeaway: Print technology accelerated religious change.
cases.title: Luther's Ninety-five Theses

cases.summary: The UN General Assembly adopted the declaration, drafted by a committee chaired by Eleanor Roosevelt, by 48 votes to none with 8 abstentions.
cases.takeaway: A non-binding declaration became the base of international human-rights law.
cases.title: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights

cases.summary: The Germanic general Odoacer deposed Emperor Romulus Augustulus in 476; the Eastern Roman (Byzantine) Empire continued until 1453.
cases.takeaway: Empires can decline gradually before a symbolic end date.
cases.title: The fall of the Western Roman Empire
cases.wiki: Fall of the Western Roman Empire

cases.summary: Tsar Nicholas II abdicated in February 1917; the Bolsheviks seized power in the October Revolution and won a civil war by 1922.
cases.takeaway: War, hunger and weak government can topple a regime.
cases.title: The Russian Revolutions of 1917

cases.summary: Copernicus's sun-centred model (1543), Galileo's telescope observations (1610) and Newton's Principia (1687) replaced Aristotelian physics.
cases.takeaway: Observation and mathematics became the basis of science.
cases.title: From Copernicus to Newton

cases.summary: Shang kings had questions to ancestors inscribed on turtle shells and ox bones, the earliest known Chinese writing.
cases.takeaway: Divination records preserved the roots of Chinese script.
cases.title: Oracle bones

cases.summary: Adults are generally advised to sleep at least seven hours a night; chronic short sleep is linked to higher risks of heart disease, diabetes and accidents.
cases.takeaway: Sleep is a basic part of health, not a luxury.
cases.title: Sleep and health

cases.summary: John Snow mapped cholera deaths in Soho, London around the Broad Street pump and persuaded officials to remove its handle.
cases.takeaway: Mapping disease reveals its source.
cases.title: John Snow's cholera map

cases.summary: The Song era saw movable-type printing (Bi Sheng, c. 1040), gunpowder weapons, navigational compasses and the first widely used paper money.
cases.takeaway: Technology and commerce flourished under a bureaucratic state.
cases.title: Song innovations

cases.summary: A Moroccan army armed with gunpowder weapons defeated Songhai at Tondibi in 1591; Timbuktu had been a centre of Islamic scholarship and trade.
cases.takeaway: Firearms changed the balance of power in West Africa.
cases.title: The fall of Songhai

cases.summary: The Soviet Union launched Sputnik on 4 October 1957; Yuri Gagarin became the first human in space in 1961; the US landed astronauts on the Moon on 20 July 1969.
cases.takeaway: Rivalry can drive rapid technological progress.
cases.title: Sputnik to the Moon

cases.summary: Nationalists led by General Franco fought the Republic; the bombing of Guernica on 26 April 1937 became a symbol of civilian suffering. Franco ruled until 1975.
cases.takeaway: Foreign intervention and ideology turned a civil war into a rehearsal for world war.
cases.title: The Spanish Civil War

cases.summary: Stalin forced peasants onto collective farms; the resulting famine killed millions, including an estimated 3.5 to 5 million in Ukraine (the Holodomor).
cases.takeaway: Rapid central planning can cause human catastrophe.
cases.title: Collectivisation and famine in the USSR

cases.summary: After Egypt nationalised the Suez Canal, Britain, France and Israel invaded; US and Soviet pressure forced them to withdraw, showing the decline of the old colonial powers.
cases.takeaway: Superpowers, not empires, now set the limits.
cases.title: The Suez Crisis

cases.summary: New Zealand became the first self-governing country to give women the vote in national elections; the UK followed in 1918 (partly) and 1928 (fully), the US in 1920.
cases.takeaway: Reform spread country by country over decades.
cases.title: New Zealand gives women the vote

cases.summary: Britain and France secretly agreed to divide the Ottoman Arab lands into spheres of influence; the borders that followed shaped the modern Middle East.
cases.takeaway: Imposed borders can leave long-lasting grievances.
cases.title: The Sykes–Picot Agreement

cases.summary: A civil war led by Hong Xiuquan, who claimed to be Jesus's younger brother, killed an estimated 20 million or more people, making it one of the deadliest wars in history.
cases.takeaway: Religious movements and social grievance can shake an empire.
cases.title: The Taiping Rebellion

cases.summary: Japan strictly limited foreign contact, allowing only Dutch and Chinese trade at Nagasaki until Commodore Perry's fleet arrived in 1853.
cases.takeaway: Isolation preserved peace but delayed technology.
cases.title: Japan's seclusion (sakoku)

cases.summary: Camel caravans carried salt and goods south across the Sahara and returned with gold, spreading Islam and linking West Africa to North African markets.
cases.takeaway: Desert routes were trade highways.
cases.title: The gold–salt trade

cases.summary: Mikhail Gorbachev resigned on 25 December and the Soviet Union ceased to exist the next day, leaving fifteen independent states.
cases.takeaway: Reform and economic stagnation undermined a superpower.
cases.title: The dissolution of the Soviet Union

cases.summary: After Napoleon's defeat, Britain, Austria, Prussia and Russia redrew Europe's map to keep a balance of power; the great powers did not fight one another again until 1914.
cases.takeaway: A balance of power can keep peace, but may suppress nationalism.
cases.title: The Congress of Vienna

cases.summary: US involvement escalated after the Gulf of Tonkin incident in 1964. The US withdrew its combat troops in 1973, and Saigon fell on 30 April 1975.
cases.takeaway: Military power did not guarantee political success.
cases.title: The Vietnam War

cases.summary: Norse raiders attacked the English monastery, marking the traditional start of the Viking Age; later settlers reached Iceland, Greenland and Newfoundland.
cases.takeaway: Seafaring raiders became traders and settlers.
cases.title: The raid on Lindisfarne

cases.summary: After a confused announcement, East Germany opened its borders and crowds crossed the Wall; Germany reunified on 3 October 1990.
cases.takeaway: Peaceful protest can end a regime.
cases.title: The fall of the Berlin Wall

cases.summary: Beginning with the Defenestration of Prague, the war drew in most of Europe and devastated the Holy Roman Empire. The Peace of Westphalia is often seen as the root of the modern system of sovereign states.
cases.takeaway: Ending a religious war led to the idea of state sovereignty.
cases.title: The Thirty Years' War

cases.summary: The General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (1947) lowered tariffs through negotiating rounds; the World Trade Organization replaced it on 1 January 1995 with a binding dispute-settlement system.
cases.takeaway: Rules-based trade grew out of postwar cooperation.
cases.title: From GATT to the WTO

cases.summary: The assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand in Sarajevo set off the July Crisis; alliance commitments pulled in Austria-Hungary, Germany, Russia, France and Britain. About 20 million people died.
cases.takeaway: Alliances and miscalculation can turn a local crisis into a world war.
cases.title: Outbreak of the First World War

cases.summary: Germany's invasion of Poland on 1 September 1939 began the war; it ended with Germany's surrender in May 1945 and Japan's in September. An estimated 70–85 million people died.
cases.takeaway: Total war mobilised whole economies and ended with new international institutions.
cases.title: The Second World War

cases.summary: An uprising at Wuchang on 10 October 1911 spread across China; the last Qing emperor abdicated in February 1912 and the Republic of China began.
cases.takeaway: Two thousand years of imperial rule ended in months.
cases.title: The Xinhai Revolution

cases.summary: Slovenia and Croatia declared independence in 1991, followed by war in Bosnia (1992–95), including the Srebrenica massacre of about 8,000 Bosniak men and boys in July 1995.
cases.takeaway: Nationalism can tear apart a multi-ethnic state.
cases.title: The breakup of Yugoslavia

cases.summary: A stone-walled capital of a Shona kingdom, built without mortar, it grew rich trading gold and ivory with Swahili ports on the Indian Ocean.
cases.takeaway: African states were part of long-distance trade networks.
cases.title: Great Zimbabwe

cases.summary: Muhammad al-Bukhari, who died in 870, reportedly examined some 600,000 reports and kept about 7,000 (with repetitions) in his Sahih.
cases.takeaway: Isnad criticism applied rigorous source checking.
cases.title: Al-Bukhari's collection

tables.title: The four Sunni schools of law
Four aims of life in Hindu thought (purusharthas)

cases.summary: An international tribunal tried leading Nazis for war crimes and crimes against humanity, establishing principles of individual responsibility.
cases.takeaway: No one is above international law.
cases.title: The Nuremberg trials

cases.summary: Bertrand Russell's chicken is fed every day and infers it always will be, until the day its neck is wrung.
cases.takeaway: Past regularity does not guarantee future events.
cases.title: Russell's chicken

formulas.label: Laplace's rule of succession
formulas.note: After s successes in n trials

cases.summary: Iceland's three largest banks failed within a week, the krona lost about half its value, and capital controls lasted until 2017.
cases.takeaway: A banking system far larger than the economy cannot be bailed out.
cases.title: Iceland's banking collapse

cases.summary: Greece received its first €110 billion bailout in May 2010, followed by further rescue programmes and austerity.
cases.takeaway: Monetary union without fiscal union is fragile.
cases.title: Greece's sovereign debt crisis

cases.summary: Claude Shannon founded information theory and showed reliable communication is possible up to the channel capacity.
cases.takeaway: Noise limits rate but not reliability.
cases.title: A Mathematical Theory of Communication

formulas.label: Shannon entropy
formulas.note: Bits of uncertainty

formulas.expr: D(P‖Q) = Σ P(x) log( P(x) / Q(x) )
formulas.label: Kullback–Leibler divergence

cases.summary: Phoenician traders used 22 letters for consonant sounds; the Greeks added vowels, and the Latin alphabet used in English developed from it.
cases.takeaway: One simple writing system spread across the world.
cases.title: The Phoenician alphabet

cases.summary: Archimedes trapped π between 223/71 and 22/7; in 2022 a team using Google Cloud calculated π to 100 trillion digits.
cases.takeaway: π is the same for every circle.
cases.title: Counting the digits of π

formulas.label: Area and circumference of a circle

formulas.expr: A = l × w,   A = ½ × b × h
formulas.label: Rectangle and triangle

cases.summary: Scientists fired tiny particles at thin gold foil; most passed straight through but a few bounced back, showing that an atom is mostly empty space with a tiny, dense nucleus.
cases.takeaway: A surprising result changed the model of the atom.
cases.title: Rutherford's gold foil experiment

cases.summary: Luc Léger designed the multistage fitness test, in which runners keep pace with beeps that get faster, to estimate aerobic fitness.
cases.takeaway: Fitness can be measured.
cases.title: The beep test

cases.summary: Gottfried Leibniz described a number system using only 0 and 1, which is how computers store all information today.
cases.takeaway: Everything on a computer is made of 0s and 1s.
cases.title: Leibniz and binary

formulas.label: Values with n bits
formulas.note: 8 bits can store 256 different values

formulas.expr: savings = income − spending,   I = P × r × t
formulas.label: Savings and simple interest
formulas.note: P principal, r yearly rate (as a decimal), t years

cases.summary: After three years of drought, Cape Town in South Africa neared the day its taps would be turned off; strict limits of 50 litres of water per person per day helped avoid it.
cases.takeaway: Everyone's choices matter in a water crisis.
cases.title: Cape Town's 'Day Zero'

cases.summary: Farmers digging a well near Xi'an, China found life-size clay soldiers buried with China's first emperor over 2,000 years ago; thousands of figures have been found.
cases.takeaway: Archaeology can be discovered by accident.
cases.title: The Terracotta Army

cases.summary: Harvey measured how much blood the heart pumps and showed that it must go round in a circle, rather than being made fresh and used up.
cases.takeaway: Measuring and calculating can overturn old ideas.
cases.title: William Harvey and the heart

cases.summary: Benjamin Franklin reportedly flew a kite in a thunderstorm to show that lightning is electricity; the experiment was dangerous and others who tried it were killed.
cases.takeaway: Lightning is a giant electric spark.
cases.title: Franklin's kite

formulas.label: Ohm's law
formulas.note: Voltage in volts = current in amps × resistance in ohms

cases.summary: Thirty-nine delegates signed the document that set up the United States government, with three branches that check each other's power.
cases.takeaway: A written constitution sets limits on power.
cases.title: The US Constitution is signed

cases.summary: The story says Archimedes realised, in his bath, that he could test whether a crown was pure gold by measuring the water it displaced; he shouted 'Eureka!'
cases.takeaway: Density can identify a material.
cases.title: Archimedes and the golden crown

formulas.label: Density
formulas.note: Mass divided by volume; water is 1 g/cm³

cases.summary: Cave paintings and dry lake beds show that the Sahara once had grasslands, lakes and animals such as hippos, during a wetter period called the African Humid Period.
cases.takeaway: Even deserts have changed with climate.
cases.title: A green Sahara

cases.summary: A fur trader named Alexis St. Martin was shot in the stomach and survived with an opening that never fully closed; Dr William Beaumont used it to watch and test how the stomach digests food.
cases.takeaway: Careful observation taught us how digestion works.
cases.title: A window into the stomach

cases.summary: Built for Pharaoh Khufu from about 2.3 million blocks, it was originally about 146 m tall and was the tallest human-made structure for roughly 3,800 years.
cases.takeaway: Ancient Egyptians organised enormous building projects.
cases.title: The Great Pyramid of Giza

cases.summary: Humphry Davy passed electricity through molten potash and soda and isolated the metals potassium and sodium for the first time.
cases.takeaway: Electricity can break compounds apart.
cases.title: Davy discovers sodium and potassium

cases.summary: Frederick Banting and Charles Best found a hormone that controls blood sugar; in January 1922 a 14-year-old boy, Leonard Thompson, became the first person with diabetes to be treated with it.
cases.takeaway: Understanding a hormone turned a deadly illness into a manageable one.
cases.title: The discovery of insulin

cases.summary: Plants capture the Sun's energy; when a rabbit eats a plant and a fox eats the rabbit, only about a tenth of the energy passes to each next level, so food chains rarely have more than four or five links.
cases.takeaway: Energy is lost at every step of a food chain.
cases.title: A simple food chain

charts.note: Illustrative numbers using the '10% rule': plants (producers), rabbits (primary consumers), foxes (secondary) and eagles (tertiary); about a tenth of energy passes up each level.
charts.title: Energy passed up a food chain

cases.summary: One of the first electronic general-purpose computers, ENIAC used about 18,000 vacuum tubes and weighed about 30 tonnes, yet a phone today is vastly more powerful.
cases.takeaway: Computers have shrunk while their power has grown enormously.
cases.title: ENIAC

cases.summary: The heavier a shopping trolley, the harder you must push to speed it up; doubling the force doubles the acceleration, and doubling the mass halves it.
cases.takeaway: Force, mass and acceleration are linked.
cases.title: Weighing a rocket

formulas.label: Newton's second law
formulas.note: Force in newtons = mass in kg × acceleration in m/s²

cases.summary: Cold, windless weather trapped smoke from coal fires over London for five days; thousands of people died, which led to the Clean Air Act of 1956.
cases.takeaway: Burning fuels releases pollution that harms health.
cases.title: The Great Smog of London

formulas.label: Burning methane
formulas.note: A fuel plus oxygen gives carbon dioxide and water

cases.summary: Mahatma Gandhi led thousands on a 390 km walk to the sea at Dandi to make salt in defiance of the British salt tax, a landmark of non-violent protest in India's independence movement.
cases.takeaway: Peaceful protest can challenge unjust laws.
cases.title: The Salt March

cases.summary: Robert Koch showed that a bacterium causes tuberculosis, and set out steps for proving that a germ causes a disease; he later identified the cholera bacterium.
cases.takeaway: Specific germs cause specific diseases.
cases.title: Robert Koch finds the cause of tuberculosis

cases.summary: According to Newton's own later account, watching an apple fall made him wonder whether the force that pulls apples also holds the Moon in orbit.
cases.takeaway: One force explains both falling apples and orbits.
cases.title: Newton and the apple

formulas.label: Weight
formulas.note: g ≈ 9.8 N/kg on Earth and about 1.6 N/kg on the Moon, so mass stays the same but weight changes

cases.summary: The ancient Greeks held athletic contests at Olympia every four years in honour of Zeus; wars were paused so athletes could travel safely.
cases.takeaway: Sport can bring people together.
cases.title: The first Olympic Games

cases.summary: Dr Ignaz Semmelweis asked doctors in a Vienna hospital to wash their hands in chlorinated lime, and deaths of mothers after childbirth fell from roughly 10% to about 2%.
cases.takeaway: Clean hands save lives.
cases.title: Semmelweis and handwashing

cases.summary: The iron tower expands in hot weather and can be up to about 15 cm taller in summer than in winter.
cases.takeaway: Materials expand when heated.
cases.title: The Eiffel Tower grows in summer

formulas.label: Heat energy
formulas.note: Specific heat capacity of water c = 4,200 J/kg/°C

cases.summary: At the Last Glacial Maximum huge ice sheets covered much of North America and northern Europe, and sea level was about 120 m lower than today.
cases.takeaway: Climate has changed dramatically in the past.
cases.title: The last ice age

cases.summary: Wladimir Köppen classified world climates by temperature and rainfall using the natural vegetation in each region; his system is still widely used.
cases.takeaway: Vegetation reflects climate.
cases.title: Köppen's climate map

cases.summary: John Harrison built a marine clock accurate enough for sailors to work out their longitude at sea, solving a problem that had caused many shipwrecks.
cases.takeaway: Accurate time gives position.
cases.title: Solving the longitude problem

cases.summary: Isaac Newton passed sunlight through a glass prism and showed that white light is a mixture of the colours of the rainbow.
cases.takeaway: White light is made of many colours.
cases.title: Newton splits white light

cases.summary: The story says René Descartes, lying in bed, watched a fly on the ceiling and realised its position could be described by two numbers, the idea of coordinates.
cases.takeaway: Numbers can describe position, joining algebra and geometry.
cases.title: Descartes and the fly

formulas.label: Straight line
formulas.note: m is the slope (gradient) and c is where the line crosses the y-axis

cases.summary: Michael Faraday moved a magnet through a coil of wire and made an electric current flow, the principle behind electric generators.
cases.takeaway: Moving magnets can make electricity.
cases.title: Faraday makes electricity from magnetism

cases.summary: A radio drama about a Martian invasion, presented as news bulletins, led some listeners to think it was real, an early lesson in how media can mislead.
cases.takeaway: Check sources and think about how a message is made.
cases.title: 'The War of the Worlds' broadcast
cases.wiki: The War of the Worlds (1938 radio drama)

cases.summary: Before a cheap way to extract aluminium was found in 1886, it was so rare that Napoleon III reportedly served his most honoured guests with aluminium cutlery, and it capped the Washington Monument in 1884.
cases.takeaway: A new method can turn a rare metal into a common one.
cases.title: Aluminium, once more precious than gold

cases.summary: The Lydians, in what is now Turkey, made some of the first stamped metal coins, which made trading easier than swapping goods.
cases.takeaway: Money solves the problems of barter.
cases.title: The first coins

cases.summary: As soot from factories darkened tree bark in industrial England, dark peppered moths went from rare to the majority because pale ones were easier for birds to see; clean-air laws later reversed the trend.
cases.takeaway: Natural selection can be seen within a lifetime.
cases.title: The peppered moth

cases.summary: Usain Bolt ran 100 metres in 9.58 seconds in Berlin, an average speed of about 10.4 metres per second, or about 37.6 km/h.
cases.takeaway: Speed is distance divided by time.
cases.title: Usain Bolt's world record

formulas.label: Speed
formulas.note: Distance divided by time

cases.summary: The Indian mathematician Brahmagupta wrote down rules for calculating with zero and negative numbers, treating debts as negative numbers.
cases.takeaway: Negative numbers began as a way to record debts.
cases.title: Brahmagupta and negative numbers

cases.summary: Volvo engineer Nils Bohlin invented the three-point seat belt, and Volvo gave away the patent; it keeps passengers from continuing to move forward when a car stops suddenly.
cases.takeaway: Objects keep moving unless a force stops them.
cases.title: The three-point seat belt

cases.summary: Robert Goddard launched a rocket fuelled with petrol and liquid oxygen in Massachusetts; it flew for 2.5 seconds, pushing gas down and itself up.
cases.takeaway: Every action has an equal and opposite reaction.
cases.title: The first liquid-fuel rocket

cases.summary: Florentine architect Filippo Brunelleschi showed how to draw buildings so that parallel lines meet at a vanishing point, and Masaccio used it in his Holy Trinity fresco around 1427.
cases.takeaway: Mathematics helped artists create depth.
cases.title: Brunelleschi's perspective

cases.summary: Søren Sørensen, working at the Carlsberg brewery, introduced the pH scale to measure how acidic or alkaline a liquid is.
cases.takeaway: pH 7 is neutral; below 7 is acidic and above 7 is alkaline.
cases.title: The pH scale

charts.note: Typical approximate values.
charts.title: The pH of everyday substances

cases.summary: A collection of 154 sonnets by Shakespeare was published in 1609; each has fourteen lines with a set rhyme pattern.
cases.takeaway: A strict form can shape powerful poetry.
cases.title: Shakespeare's sonnets

cases.summary: Leo Baekeland invented Bakelite, the first fully synthetic plastic, used for telephones, radios and electrical parts because it does not conduct electricity or melt easily.
cases.takeaway: New materials change everyday life.
cases.title: Bakelite

cases.summary: The United Nations estimated that the world population reached 8 billion on 15 November 2022, with people packed most densely in South and East Asia.
cases.takeaway: Population is unevenly spread across the planet.
cases.title: Eight billion people

formulas.label: Population density
formulas.note: e.g. people per square kilometre

cases.summary: Jacques Piccard and Don Walsh took the bathyscaphe Trieste to the bottom of the Challenger Deep, about 10,900 m down, where the water pressure is over 1,000 times atmospheric pressure.
cases.takeaway: Pressure increases with depth.
cases.title: Down to the deepest place in the ocean

formulas.label: Pressure
formulas.note: Force divided by area, in pascals (N/m²)

cases.summary: Eratosthenes found all the prime numbers up to any limit by crossing out the multiples of each prime in turn; Euclid had already proved there are infinitely many primes.
cases.takeaway: A simple method can find all primes.
cases.title: The Sieve of Eratosthenes

cases.summary: In a room of just 23 people there is about a 50.7% chance that two share a birthday, much higher than most people expect.
cases.takeaway: Chance behaves in surprising ways.
cases.title: The birthday problem

formulas.note: Always between 0 (impossible) and 1 (certain)

cases.summary: A Babylonian clay tablet lists sets of numbers that form right-angled triangles, showing people knew the rule over a thousand years before Pythagoras.
cases.takeaway: Mathematics was developed in many cultures.
cases.title: Plimpton 322

formulas.note: c is the longest side (hypotenuse) of a right-angled triangle

cases.summary: Henri Becquerel found that uranium salts darkened photographic plates even in the dark, the first sign of radioactivity.
cases.takeaway: Some atoms give off energy on their own.
cases.title: Becquerel discovers radioactivity

cases.summary: Ramadan is the ninth month of the Islamic lunar calendar; because a lunar year is about 354 days, it begins about 10 to 11 days earlier each year in the Gregorian calendar.
cases.takeaway: Lunar calendars drift against the seasons.
cases.title: A month that moves through the year

cases.summary: Antoine Lavoisier weighed everything before and after reactions in sealed containers and showed that the total mass does not change.
cases.takeaway: Atoms are rearranged in a reaction, not created or destroyed.
cases.title: Lavoisier and the conservation of mass

formulas.label: A balanced equation
formulas.note: Same number of each type of atom on both sides

cases.summary: Plato imagined prisoners who only see shadows on a cave wall and think the shadows are real; one escapes and sees the world outside.
cases.takeaway: Things may not be what they seem.
cases.title: The Allegory of the Cave

cases.summary: Martin Luther King Jr. delivered his speech to about 250,000 people at the March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom, calling for an end to racial discrimination.
cases.takeaway: Words and peaceful protest can change laws.
cases.title: 'I Have a Dream'

cases.summary: Spring floods burst levees along the Mississippi and displaced about 700,000 people, prompting the US government to take a much larger role in flood control.
cases.takeaway: Flood control needs planning along the whole river.
cases.title: The Great Mississippi Flood

cases.summary: A clay tablet known as YBC 7289 shows a square with its diagonal marked and an approximation of √2 accurate to about six decimal places.
cases.takeaway: People have calculated roots for nearly 4,000 years.
cases.title: A Babylonian square root

cases.summary: The statue's copper skin was bright and brown when it was built in 1886; over about 30 years air and rain formed a green layer, called a patina, that now protects the metal.
cases.takeaway: Some corrosion protects, while rusting on iron destroys.
cases.title: The Statue of Liberty turns green

formulas.label: Rusting of iron
formulas.note: Iron needs both oxygen and water to rust

cases.summary: The average distance from Earth to the Sun is 149,600,000 km, written as 1.496 × 10⁸ km in scientific notation, which makes very large or small numbers easy to handle.
cases.takeaway: Scientific notation shortens huge and tiny numbers.
cases.title: How far is the Sun?

cases.summary: In the old story, a wise man asks a king for one grain of wheat on the first square of a chessboard, doubled on each next square; by the last square the total is over 18 quintillion grains, far more than has ever been grown.
cases.takeaway: Doubling grows very fast.
cases.title: Wheat on a chessboard

charts.note: The numbers double each square: 1, 2, 4, 8, …

formulas.note: d is the common difference; r is the common ratio

cases.summary: The English logician John Venn introduced the overlapping-circle diagrams that now bear his name to show how groups of things relate.
cases.takeaway: Pictures can make logic clear.
cases.title: John Venn's diagrams

cases.summary: Scientists in Ethiopia found about 40% of the skeleton of an early human relative who lived 3.2 million years ago; she walked upright, which her pelvis and leg bones showed.
cases.takeaway: Bones are evidence of how our ancestors lived.
cases.title: Lucy's skeleton

cases.summary: Richard Doll and Austin Bradford Hill followed tens of thousands of British doctors and found that smokers were far more likely to die of lung cancer.
cases.takeaway: Large studies show cause and risk.
cases.title: Smoking and lung cancer

cases.summary: Socrates spent his life asking people questions to test their beliefs; Athens condemned him to death and he chose to drink hemlock rather than escape.
cases.takeaway: Asking questions is the heart of philosophy.
cases.title: The trial of Socrates

cases.summary: The International Astronomical Union defined 'planet' and moved Pluto to the new class of dwarf planets because it has not cleared other objects from its orbit.
cases.takeaway: Scientists change categories when new evidence arrives.
cases.title: Pluto is reclassified

charts.note: 1 astronomical unit (AU) is the average Earth–Sun distance, about 150 million km.
charts.title: Distance of each planet from the Sun

cases.summary: Pilot Chuck Yeager flew the Bell X-1 faster than the speed of sound, about 343 m/s in air at 20 °C, over the California desert.
cases.takeaway: Sound travels at a fixed speed through air.
cases.title: Breaking the sound barrier

formulas.label: Wave speed
formulas.note: Speed = frequency × wavelength

cases.summary: William Herschel put thermometers in the colours of a prism spectrum and found that the one just beyond the red end got warmest, showing invisible 'heat rays'.
cases.takeaway: There is light we cannot see.
cases.title: Herschel discovers infrared

cases.summary: Nightingale drew a coloured chart showing that far more soldiers in the Crimean War died from disease than from wounds, which helped persuade the government to improve hospitals.
cases.takeaway: A clear chart can change minds.
cases.title: Florence Nightingale's rose diagram

cases.summary: The storm flooded most of New Orleans when its levees failed and caused about 1,800 deaths, showing how poor defences and planning raise the harm from a natural hazard.
cases.takeaway: Preparation reduces disaster damage.
cases.title: Hurricane Katrina

cases.summary: Artists decorated the Alhambra palace in Spain with repeating tile patterns that use many kinds of symmetry; the artist M. C. Escher studied them there in 1922.
cases.takeaway: Art and mathematics meet in patterns.
cases.title: The Alhambra's tilings

cases.summary: Venice began charging day-trippers an entry fee of €5 on busy days, to limit crowding in a city of only about 50,000 residents.
cases.takeaway: Tourism brings money and pressure on places.
cases.title: Venice charges day visitors

cases.summary: Surveyors of the Great Trigonometrical Survey of India used angles and triangles from hundreds of kilometres away to calculate the height of Peak XV, later named Mount Everest, as 29,002 feet.
cases.takeaway: Trigonometry measures what you cannot reach.
cases.title: Measuring Mount Everest

cases.summary: Fifty-one countries joined the UN after the Second World War to keep peace and encourage cooperation; today it has 193 members.
cases.takeaway: Countries created an organisation to prevent another world war.
cases.title: The United Nations is founded

cases.summary: According to the United Nations, 2007 was the first year when more than half of the world's people lived in towns and cities.
cases.takeaway: The world has become mostly urban.
cases.title: More people in cities than in the countryside

cases.summary: About 97% of Earth's water is salty ocean water and about 2% is frozen in ice caps and glaciers, leaving less than 1% as fresh liquid water for people, plants and animals.
cases.takeaway: Fresh water is a precious, limited resource.
cases.title: Where Earth's water is

cases.summary: Archimedes is said to have claimed that with a long enough lever and a place to stand he could move the Earth, to show how levers multiply force.
cases.takeaway: Machines trade a longer push for a smaller force.
cases.title: 'Give me a place to stand'

cases.takeaway: Social solidarity helps explain political power.

cases.summary: US emission rules led to catalytic converters using platinum-group metals, converting CO, hydrocarbons and NOx into CO₂, H₂O and N₂.
cases.takeaway: A catalyst can cut pollution without changing the fuel.

cases.title: Lorenz and the butterfly effect

cases.summary: The JPEG standard compresses images by transforming 8×8 pixel blocks into frequencies and discarding those the eye barely notices.
cases.takeaway: Transforms split data into parts that can be compressed.
cases.title: JPEG compression

cases.summary: Euclid organised geometry into definitions, axioms and proofs; the Elements was a standard textbook for more than 2,000 years.
cases.takeaway: Proof from axioms is the model of mathematical reasoning.
cases.title: Euclid's Elements

cases.summary: Leonhard Euler proved that no walk could cross each of the city's seven bridges exactly once, founding graph theory.
cases.takeaway: Abstracting a problem to dots and lines reveals its structure.
cases.title: The Seven Bridges of Königsberg

cases.summary: Ernő Rubik invented the cube in 1974; it has 43,252,003,274,489,856,000 positions, and in 2010 computers proved any position can be solved in at most 20 moves.
cases.takeaway: Group theory describes a puzzle's symmetries.
cases.title: The Rubik's Cube

cases.summary: Larry Page and Sergey Brin ranked web pages using the principal eigenvector of a matrix of links, the idea behind Google's early search results.
cases.takeaway: Linear algebra can organise the Web.
cases.title: PageRank

cases.summary: Kurt Gödel proved that any consistent formal system containing arithmetic has true statements it cannot prove, ending hopes of a complete foundation for mathematics.
cases.takeaway: Every formal system has limits.
cases.title: Gödel's incompleteness theorems

cases.summary: George Dantzig devised the simplex method for linear programming while working on US Air Force planning; it still underlies logistics and scheduling software.
cases.takeaway: Optimisation methods allocate scarce resources.
cases.title: The simplex algorithm

cases.summary: Luke Durant found the Mersenne prime 2^136,279,841 − 1, which has 41,024,320 digits, using cloud GPUs through the Great Internet Mersenne Prime Search.
cases.takeaway: Primes remain an open frontier.
cases.title: The largest known prime

cases.summary: Marilyn vos Savant's answer that switching doors wins 2/3 of the time drew thousands of letters from readers, including mathematicians, who insisted she was wrong; simulations proved her right.
cases.takeaway: Probability intuition can fail, even for experts.
cases.title: The Monty Hall problem

cases.summary: Ransomware using the leaked EternalBlue exploit infected hundreds of thousands of computers in about 150 countries and disrupted UK hospitals; a kill-switch domain slowed it.

cases.summary: The US National Resident Matching Program adopted a deferred-acceptance algorithm; Alvin Roth and Lloyd Shapley won the 2012 Nobel Prize in economics for matching theory.

cases.summary: Researchers matched 'anonymous' Netflix ratings with public IMDb reviews to identify users.
cases.takeaway: Removing names does not make data anonymous.
cases.title: Netflix Prize de-anonymisation

cases.summary: The Census Bureau adopted differential privacy to protect respondents, prompting debate about accuracy for small areas.
cases.takeaway: Privacy protection has measurable accuracy costs.
cases.title: US Census 2020 and differential privacy

formulas.label: ε-differential privacy

formulas.label: Laplace mechanism
formulas.note: Δf is the sensitivity of f

cases.summary: Experiments by Clauser, Aspect and Zeilinger showed that quantum correlations violate Bell inequalities, ruling out local hidden variables; they shared the 2022 Nobel Prize in Physics.
cases.takeaway: Entanglement is a real, testable feature of nature.
cases.title: Bell test experiments

formulas.label: Particle in a box
formulas.note: Quantised energy levels

cases.summary: Peter Shor showed a quantum computer could factor large integers in polynomial time, threatening RSA.
cases.takeaway: Quantum computing motivates post-quantum cryptography.
cases.title: Shor's algorithm

cases.summary: Google reported a 53-qubit processor performing a sampling task in about 200 seconds that it estimated would take a supercomputer 10,000 years; classical rivals later narrowed the gap.
cases.takeaway: Claims of quantum advantage are tested by classical improvements.
cases.title: Google's Sycamore

formulas.label: Bell state
formulas.note: Maximally entangled pair

formulas.label: Grover search speed-up
formulas.note: Quadratic speed-up over classical search

cases.summary: John Rawls proposed choosing principles of justice behind a 'veil of ignorance' about one's own position in society.
cases.takeaway: Fairness can be modelled as impartial choice.
cases.title: A Theory of Justice

formulas.expr: choose the policy maximising min uᵢ
formulas.label: Difference principle (maximin)
formulas.note: Inequalities are just only if they benefit the least advantaged

Inequalities must benefit the least advantaged
tables.title: Rawls's two principles of justice

cases.summary: The fresco in Santa Maria Novella, Florence is among the first paintings to use mathematically consistent linear perspective.
cases.takeaway: Mathematics changed how artists depict space.
cases.title: Masaccio's Holy Trinity

formulas.label: Linear perspective
formulas.note: Brunelleschi's c. 1415 demonstration; codified by Alberti in De pictura (1435)

rows: October Revolution brings the Bolsheviks to power
tables.title: Revolutions compared

cases.summary: Bernhard Riemann's eight-page paper on primes introduced the zeta-function approach and the hypothesis that still bears his name; it is a Clay Millennium Problem.
cases.takeaway: A short paper can set a research agenda for centuries.
cases.title: Riemann's 1859 paper

formulas.expr: All non-trivial zeros satisfy Re(s) = ½
formulas.label: Riemann hypothesis
formulas.note: Verified numerically for trillions of zeros but unproved

cases.summary: DeepMind's DQN learned to play 49 Atari games from pixels and reached human-level performance on many.
cases.takeaway: Deep networks plus RL can learn control from raw input.
cases.title: Deep Q-Network on Atari

cases.summary: A single algorithm trained purely by self-play mastered chess, shogi and Go.
cases.takeaway: Self-play removes the need for human data.
cases.title: AlphaZero

cases.summary: A skater who pulls in her arms spins faster, because angular momentum is conserved: a smaller radius means a larger angular speed.
cases.takeaway: Conservation laws explain familiar motion.
cases.title: The spinning figure skater

formulas.label: Angular momentum
formulas.note: Conserved when no outside torque acts, so a smaller I gives a larger ω

cases.summary: Michel Mayor and Didier Queloz announced 51 Pegasi b, a gas giant orbiting in 4 days; they shared the 2019 Nobel Prize in Physics. Thousands more exoplanets have been confirmed since.
cases.takeaway: Other planetary systems are common.
cases.title: The first exoplanet around a Sun-like star

formulas.label: Stefan–Boltzmann law
formulas.note: A star's luminosity depends on its radius and surface temperature

cases.summary: At Kitty Hawk, Orville Wright flew 120 feet in 12 seconds in a powered, controlled aircraft; their wind-tunnel data on wing shapes was the key to lift.
cases.takeaway: Careful measurement of lift and drag made flight possible.
cases.title: The Wright brothers' first flight

formulas.label: Bernoulli's equation
formulas.note: Along a streamline, faster flow means lower pressure

cases.summary: Thomas Edison's power plant in lower Manhattan began supplying direct current to about 85 customers for electric lighting, the first commercial power plant of its kind in the US.
cases.takeaway: Electric power turned a laboratory curiosity into a utility.
cases.title: Pearl Street Station

cases.summary: A geomagnetic storm induced currents in power lines and collapsed Hydro-Québec's grid in about 90 seconds, leaving six million people without power for nine hours.
cases.takeaway: Faraday's induction applies to the planet-sized scale too.
cases.title: The 1989 Québec blackout

formulas.label: Faraday's law
formulas.note: Changing magnetic flux induces an emf

cases.summary: James Joule showed that stirring water with a falling weight warmed it by a fixed amount per unit of work, giving the mechanical equivalent of heat (about 4.18 J per calorie).
cases.takeaway: Heat and work are two forms of energy.
cases.title: Joule's paddle-wheel experiment

formulas.label: Kinetic and potential energy
formulas.note: In a closed system KE + PE stays constant if friction is negligible

cases.summary: Isaac Newton published his three laws of motion and the law of universal gravitation, explaining both falling apples and planetary orbits with the same mathematics.
cases.takeaway: One set of laws governs Earth and the heavens.
cases.title: Newton's Principia

formulas.label: Newton's second law
formulas.note: Net force equals mass times acceleration

cases.summary: Charles Kao showed that glass fibre could carry light over long distances if impurities were removed; he shared the 2009 Nobel Prize. Fibre now carries most Internet traffic.
cases.takeaway: Theory plus materials science created a global network.
cases.title: Optical fibre

formulas.label: Snell's law
formulas.note: Light bends when entering a medium with a different refractive index

cases.summary: Urbain Le Verrier and John Couch Adams predicted a new planet from irregularities in Uranus's orbit; Johann Galle found Neptune within one degree of the predicted position.
cases.takeaway: Mathematics can find what telescopes have not yet seen.
cases.title: The discovery of Neptune

formulas.label: Kepler's third law
formulas.note: The square of the orbital period is proportional to the cube of the semi-major axis

cases.summary: Max Planck proposed that energy is emitted in discrete packets to explain blackbody radiation; Einstein used the idea for the photoelectric effect in 1905.
cases.takeaway: Energy comes in quanta.
cases.title: Planck's quantum

formulas.label: Wien's displacement law
formulas.note: Hotter objects peak at shorter wavelengths

cases.summary: At Bell Labs, John Bardeen and Walter Brattain built the first point-contact transistor; with William Shockley they won the 1956 Nobel Prize in Physics.
cases.takeaway: Quantum band theory made modern electronics possible.
cases.title: The invention of the transistor

cases.summary: GPS satellite clocks run about 38 microseconds a day fast relative to ground clocks (+45 from weaker gravity, −7 from speed), so engineers correct for relativity or positions would drift by kilometres a day.
cases.takeaway: Relativity is an everyday engineering fact.
cases.title: GPS and relativity
cases.wiki: Error analysis for the Global Positioning System

formulas.label: Time dilation
formulas.note: Moving clocks run slow

cases.summary: Sadi Carnot analysed steam engines and showed that efficiency depends only on the temperatures of the hot and cold reservoirs, founding thermodynamics.
cases.takeaway: No engine can be 100% efficient.
cases.title: Carnot and the heat engine

formulas.label: First law
formulas.note: Change in internal energy = heat added − work done

formulas.label: Carnot efficiency
formulas.note: Temperatures in kelvin

cases.summary: A suspension bridge in Washington state twisted and collapsed in 64 km/h winds because of aeroelastic flutter, often loosely described as resonance.
cases.takeaway: Structures must be designed for wind-driven vibration.
cases.title: The Tacoma Narrows Bridge collapse

formulas.label: Wave speed
formulas.note: Speed = frequency × wavelength

cases.summary: Ibn al-Haytham used experiments to show that vision works by light entering the eye, and is often cited as a pioneer of the experimental method.
cases.takeaway: Hypothesis plus experiment decides between theories.
cases.title: Ibn al-Haytham's Book of Optics

formulas.label: Completing the square (al-Khwarizmi)
formulas.note: From al-Jabr, c. 820

cases.summary: The Han envoy travelled west to seek allies against the Xiongnu and returned with knowledge that opened Chinese contact with Central Asia.
cases.takeaway: Diplomacy opened trade routes.
cases.title: Zhang Qian's mission

cases.summary: Genghis Khan united the Mongol tribes in 1206; at its height the empire was the largest contiguous land empire in history and secured long-distance trade.
cases.takeaway: Conquest also created safer trade corridors.
cases.title: The Mongol Empire

rows: About 12.5 million Africans were forced onto ships; about 10.7 million survived the Middle Passage (Slave Voyages database)
tables.title: Atlantic slave trade: key points

cases.summary: Robert Solow found that most of US output growth could not be explained by capital and labour, pointing to technology; he won the 1987 Nobel Prize.
cases.takeaway: Ideas, not just inputs, drive growth.
cases.title: The Solow residual

formulas.label: Convergence
formulas.note: Poorer economies grow faster, other things equal

cases.summary: Researchers including Google Project Zero revealed that speculative execution in most modern processors could leak secrets across security boundaries.
cases.takeaway: Performance optimisations can undermine security.
cases.title: Spectre and Meltdown disclosed

rows: Isolation between user programs and the kernel
Branch target prediction, via branch injection
tables.title: Spectre and Meltdown

cases.summary: Rosalind Franklin and Raymond Gosling's X-ray diffraction image of DNA provided key evidence for the helical structure.
cases.takeaway: Experimental data enabled the double-helix model.
cases.title: Photo 51

formulas.label: Beer–Lambert law
formulas.note: Absorbance is proportional to concentration

cases.summary: Einstein predicted the random jiggling of pollen grains from molecular collisions; Jean Perrin's experiments confirmed it and helped establish atoms.
cases.takeaway: Randomness at small scales reveals hidden structure.
cases.title: Einstein's explanation of Brownian motion

cases.summary: Attackers inserted malicious code into a software update that reached roughly 18,000 customers, including government agencies.
cases.takeaway: Trusted updates are an attack path.
cases.title: SolarWinds Orion compromise
cases.wiki: 2020 United States federal government data breach

cases.summary: A critical flaw in the Log4j logging library (CVE-2021-44228) allowed remote code execution in countless applications.
cases.takeaway: Know your dependencies (software bill of materials).
cases.title: Log4Shell

cases.summary: Seventeen software developers met at a ski resort in Snowbird, Utah, and wrote the Manifesto for Agile Software Development, favouring working software and responding to change over rigid plans.
cases.takeaway: Iterative delivery replaced long, plan-heavy projects.
cases.title: The Agile Manifesto

cases.summary: Grace Hopper's A-0 system translated symbolic code into machine instructions, leading to COBOL and the idea that programmers should write in near-English.
cases.takeaway: Higher-level languages made programming accessible.
cases.title: Grace Hopper's first compiler

cases.summary: Edgar F. Codd of IBM published 'A Relational Model of Data for Large Shared Data Banks', the foundation for SQL databases.
cases.takeaway: A clean mathematical model outlasts implementations.
cases.title: Codd's relational model

formulas.label: Present value
formulas.note: A dollar later is worth less than a dollar now

formulas.label: Gordon growth model
formulas.note: Value of a stream of dividends growing at g (needs r > g)

cases.summary: IBM's Deep Blue won a six-game match against world chess champion Garry Kasparov by 3½ to 2½, the first time a computer beat a reigning champion under match conditions.
cases.takeaway: Brute-force search plus evaluation can beat human experts at a narrow task.
cases.title: Deep Blue beats Kasparov

cases.summary: Researchers at Google showed that vector arithmetic on word embeddings captures analogies, such as king − man + woman ≈ queen.
cases.takeaway: Meaning can be represented as geometry.
cases.title: Word2vec

formulas.label: Word analogy
formulas.note: Nearest neighbour by cosine similarity

formulas.label: Economic order quantity
formulas.note: D annual demand, S cost per order, H holding cost per unit per year

cases.summary: Tim Berners-Lee at CERN publicly announced the World Wide Web project and its first website, info.cern.ch; CERN placed the technology in the public domain in 1993.
cases.takeaway: Open standards let the Web grow without permission.
cases.title: The first website
cases.wiki: History of the World Wide Web

cases.summary: P&G found that orders for Pampers diapers varied far more along the supply chain than actual baby consumption, which is steady, because each stage over-reacted to small changes.
cases.takeaway: Information sharing steadies supply chains.
cases.title: The bullwhip effect at Procter & Gamble

cases.summary: Google released Kubernetes as open source, based on lessons from its internal Borg system, and it became the standard way to run containers at scale.
cases.takeaway: Large-company infrastructure ideas can become shared standards.
cases.title: Kubernetes

cases.summary: KKR won a bidding war for RJR Nabisco at about $25 billion, then the largest leveraged buyout ever, using mostly borrowed money.
cases.takeaway: Debt amplifies both returns and risk.
cases.title: The RJR Nabisco buyout

cases.summary: Charley Kline at UCLA tried to log in to a computer at Stanford; the system crashed after he typed 'LO' of 'LOGIN'. The network grew into the Internet.
cases.takeaway: Big systems start with a simple, imperfect message.
cases.title: The first ARPANET message

cases.summary: Soon after landing, the rover's computer kept resetting because a low-priority task held a resource needed by a high-priority one (priority inversion); engineers uploaded a fix enabling priority inheritance from Earth.
cases.takeaway: Concurrency bugs can hide until they show up on another planet.
cases.title: The Mars Pathfinder resets

cases.summary: The US Navy developed PERT to plan the Polaris submarine missile programme, which involved thousands of contractors, and the technique spread through project management.
cases.takeaway: Network diagrams show which tasks can delay the whole project.
cases.title: PERT and the Polaris missile

formulas.label: PERT estimate
formulas.note: Optimistic, most likely and pessimistic durations

formulas.expr: CPI = EV ÷ AC,   SPI = EV ÷ PV
formulas.label: Earned value indices
formulas.note: Values below 1 mean over budget or behind schedule

cases.summary: Attackers phoned Twitter employees, tricked them into giving access to internal tools, and posted a bitcoin scam from accounts of well-known people.
cases.takeaway: People are often the weakest link, so train for social engineering.
cases.title: The 2020 Twitter account takeover

cases.summary: Harry Markowitz's paper 'Portfolio Selection' showed that combining assets that don't move together lowers risk without lowering expected return; he shared the 1990 Nobel Prize.
cases.takeaway: Don't judge an asset in isolation; judge its effect on the whole portfolio.
cases.title: Markowitz and diversification

formulas.label: Two-asset portfolio variance
formulas.note: The lower the correlation ρ, the greater the diversification benefit

cases.summary: About 6.5 million hashed passwords appeared online in 2012; in 2016 a far larger set of about 117 million was released, and many passwords were cracked because they were stored without salting.
cases.takeaway: Store passwords with salted, slow hashes and use multi-factor authentication.
cases.title: The LinkedIn password breach

formulas.label: Password strength (entropy)
formulas.note: L randomly chosen characters from an alphabet of N symbols; each extra bit doubles the guesses

cases.summary: Engineer Bill Smith developed Six Sigma at Motorola to cut defects to about 3.4 per million opportunities; General Electric later popularised it.
cases.takeaway: Measure defects to reduce them.
cases.title: Six Sigma at Motorola

cases.summary: Agner Erlang, a Danish engineer, used probability to work out how many telephone lines a town needed, founding queueing theory.
cases.takeaway: Maths can size a service to meet demand.
cases.title: Erlang and telephone exchanges

formulas.label: Little's law
formulas.note: Average number in the system = arrival rate × average time in the system

cases.summary: Enron used off-balance-sheet entities to hide debt and inflate profits; it filed for bankruptcy in December 2001 and its auditor Arthur Andersen collapsed.
cases.takeaway: Financial statements are only as reliable as the people and checks behind them.
cases.title: The Enron collapse

formulas.label: Current ratio
formulas.note: Below 1 suggests difficulty paying short-term debts

cases.summary: Alan Turing described an abstract machine that reads and writes symbols on a tape and used it to prove that some problems, such as the halting problem, cannot be solved by any algorithm.
cases.takeaway: There are precise limits to what computers can do.
cases.title: On Computable Numbers

cases.summary: Alan Turing's paper 'Computing Machinery and Intelligence' proposed judging machine intelligence by whether a person could tell its replies from a human's, the idea now called the Turing test.
cases.takeaway: Behaviour, not inner workings, became the test of intelligence.
cases.title: The imitation game

cases.summary: Fei-Fei Li's team assembled over 14 million labelled images; the annual ImageNet challenge drove the deep-learning boom after AlexNet's win in 2012.
cases.takeaway: Large, well-labelled datasets drive progress as much as algorithms.
cases.title: ImageNet

cases.summary: Charles Minard drew the shrinking size of Napoleon's army as a band that narrows from about 422,000 men to a few thousand, with temperatures plotted below; Edward Tufte called it possibly the best statistical graphic ever.
cases.takeaway: One good graphic can tell a whole story.
cases.title: Minard's map of Napoleon's Russian campaign

cases.summary: Grigori Perelman posted proofs using Ricci flow; he declined the 2006 Fields Medal and the 2010 Clay Millennium Prize of $1 million.
cases.takeaway: Open problems can be solved by new methods from analysis.
cases.title: Perelman and the Poincaré conjecture

formulas.label: Euler characteristic (surface of genus g)
formulas.note: Sphere 2, torus 0

cases.summary: Google researchers replaced recurrence with attention; the Transformer set new state-of-the-art translation scores (28.4 BLEU English–German, 41.8 English–French) while training faster.
cases.takeaway: One architecture later underpinned today's large language models.
cases.title: Attention Is All You Need

formulas.label: Sinusoidal positional encoding
formulas.note: Injects word order into a model with no recurrence

cases.summary: A trading position in credit derivatives lost about $6.2 billion, partly because a VaR model was changed using a flawed spreadsheet.
cases.takeaway: Model risk is operational risk too.
cases.title: JPMorgan 'London Whale' losses

formulas.note: Average loss in the worst tail
